The stack of BTstack's worker (6 KB) now also runs the SBC encoder and the A2DP state machine: check its minimum free stack on the bench before anything else grows. Decoder ring in Bluetooth mode is half as deep (46 ms): the bench has to show the 44.1 kHz decoders ride that out (underruns=0).

On the board (stage 2b), in this order.

  1. Y2 first: pair, Connect, play a WAV and a FLAC: sound within a second, no gaps for 10 minutes, bt: a2dp: SBC 44100 Hz, bitpool 53 ..., 328 kbit/s on the console, About > BT audio underruns 0.
  2. Pause for 10 s: the stream suspends (UART a2dp suspended), Play resumes it. Switch the headset off while playing: pause at once, banner, the position unchanged when it is back and Connect is pressed.
  3. Audio output Wired with the headset connected: nothing on Bluetooth, the wired path (null sink on the Y2, I2S on the RP2350) as before. Auto again: playback stops and the output moves.
  4. RP2350 + WI-C200: the same, plus the 6 KB worker stack minimum, core 1 underruns on I2S before and after a Bluetooth session (the ring layout comes back), Wi-Fi joining and leaving while streaming (still provisional).
  5. A 48 kHz or 96 kHz file on Bluetooth: refused with the message, the queue moves on, nothing crashes.
  6. AirPods Pro 3: Connect, music; try NEUPOD_BT_SBC_XQ=1 on a build and listen (the ADR-0007 test).

docs.title: Link robustness (built)
docs.text:
Why. A 47-minute walk on the Y2 with AirPods Pro (Y2 in a pocket, 12 Nov 2026; logs kept off-repo) gave glitches and some full breakdowns. What the firmware log showed:

  • The decoder never starved (ring_min 2048 of 2048 throughout, FLAC about 1.5 % of one core) and the encoder ring underran 8 times in 47 minutes. The audio was always there; the link was the limit.
  • Normally about 431 packets per 10 s. In bad patches the encoder waited on the link (02:14:35 to 02:14:45: only about half the audio got through). The old rule never owed the headset more than 40 ms after a stall, so every stall permanently drained the headset's jitter buffer by what the link had held up, and a few of them in a row was a glitch, then a dropout.
  • The mid-song a2dp suspended lines (3 of the walk's 12, at 02:13:47, 02:14:38 and 02:15:46; all 12 are ours, none "by the headset") were not the route going quiet while playing. Each is preceded by display: wake / backlight wake a few seconds before (a key on the Y2 itself, which in a pocket is a press of Play/Pause), the PCM frame counter freezes there (e.g. 726,528 to 741,632 frames over the next 10 s), and the stream resumes at a later Play (the headset's key PLAY at 02:13:56, or the next press). audio_route.c only suspends when the player is not PLAYING for 4 s, and it was paused. The firmware now says so: player: paused (Play/Pause) / player: playing (Play/Pause), and route: not playing for N ms (player state S), suspending the stream.
  • The a2dp stream released events at 02:22:34, 02:43:09, 02:43:16, 02:47:23 and 02:49:59 were not the headset letting go: each is followed within the same second by route: output wired, which only the Disconnect / Forget actions produce (audio_route_user_released), and then by bt: connect (a manual Connect; the automatic one logs bt: reconnecting). They are the owner's manual reconnects after a breakdown. The volume cap at 02:43:15 (66 % to 50 %) happened three times in the log with the same sequence and only that once was followed by a disconnect, a second later and by hand. Nothing in the log says the cap provoked anything. The actual cause of the breakdowns is not in the firmware log (no link-level lines). Hence the diagnostics below and the HCI trace advice.

What was built (one place for every number: hal/common/bt_btstack/bt_link_policy.h, pure functions, host tests bt_link_policy).

  1. Bounded catch-up. The owed-audio cap is now BT_LINK_CATCHUP_MS = 160 ms. After a stall the missed audio is encoded and sent as fast as the link takes packets (one packet per 8 ms tick at most, about 3 times real time), so the headset's buffer fills again. There is no unbounded burst; audio owed beyond the budget is forgone and counted (drops). In practice the ring is what limits it: the Bluetooth ring holds 93 ms and the audio core waits, losing nothing, while it is full (see above), so up to about 93 ms of a stall can be made up; the budget is headroom for a larger ring. A ring that runs dry while paying off a stall is the catch-up having caught up, not an underrun. The start-up burst keeps the old 40 ms bound.
  2. Adaptive bitpool. One tick is pressured when the packet has waited 30 ms for "can send now" or 50 ms of audio is owed. A 1 s window with 25 % pressured ticks is bad; 2 bad windows in a row step the bitpool down 53, 45, 35 (never above what the headset asks for, never below its minimum; steps that coincide are one; with NEUPOD_BT_SBC_XQ the ladder starts at 76). The encoder is reconfigured between two frames (set_bitpool): SBC frames carry their bitpool, so the headset needs no AVDTP reconfigure (the frames of a packet in progress keep their own length: g_sbc_frames). It steps back up one level after 15 s without a bad window and under 5 % pressure; a step down soon (60 s) after a step up doubles the hold (to 60 s at most), so a link that stays bad does not oscillate. Every stream start begins at the best bitpool. Every change is logged: bt: a2dp: bitpool 53 -> 45 (link backpressure), frame 103 bytes, 284 kbit/s; the Now Playing / Settings codec readout follows (it is the same published codec record). Bitrates: 53 is 328 kbit/s, 45 is 284, 35 is 229. The switch re-initialises the SBC encoder's filter state: expect at most a tick-sized discontinuity, which is far less than the dropout it prevents.
  3. Diagnostics, every 10 s (UART / Y2 log), next to the existing bt: a2dp: packets ... line:

bt: link: rssi -4 dB, wait avg/max 3/41 ms, inflight 3/4, bitpool 53, stalls 2, catchup 88 ms, drops 0 ms

  • rssi: the result of gap_read_rssi (the line is printed when the HCI answer arrives; ? if it never does). BR/EDR Read RSSI is in dB relative to the controller's golden receive power range (0 inside it, negative below it); some controllers report absolute dBm. What the MT6582 returns is one thing to learn from the next walk.
  • wait avg/max: request to the "can send now" event, of the packets sent in the window. inflight N/T: the most ACL packets the controller had outstanding at an 8 ms tick, of the T buffers it reported (HCI Read Buffer Size; 4 on the MT6582, logged once as bt: controller ACL buffers). N = T all the time means the controller's buffers are the bottleneck.
  • stalls: episodes of owing more than 40 ms (counted once per episode, not per tick). catchup: the most audio owed, ms (up to 160). drops: audio forgone beyond the budget, ms.
  • Releases and link loss are explained in the log: bt: acl down, reason 0x08 (link supervision timeout: ...), rssi, last packet N ms ago; bt: a2dp stream released (by the headset | by us; acl up | down; rssi; last packet N ms ago; bitpool); bt: disconnecting (requested by the app ...) when Disconnect / Forget does it.
  • Track names: a library queue's entries have no name until the storage task resolves them, so the queue line reads ''; the resolved file is now logged: player: file '/Music/...' (and player: next (gapless look-ahead) '...').
  • HCI trace for a walk (Y2). NEUPOD_BT_HCI_DUMP=<file> in /etc/neupod-fw.env writes a PacketLogger trace of the whole session. For an hour-long walk write it to the persistent ext4, not /tmp (RAM, and gone on a reboot):

mkdir -p /opt/neupod-logs        # once
echo 'NEUPOD_BT_HCI_DUMP=/opt/neupod-logs/hci-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).pklg' >> /etc/neupod-fw.env   # sourced by the init script, so the date is the start time
/etc/init.d/S91neupod-fw restart
The file grows by about 40 KB/s while streaming (about 150 MB per hour: check df /opt first). The port keeps a second descriptor of the file and fsync()s it every 5 s from a helper thread (no RTOS call), so the trace is on the disk to within 5 s even if the Y2 loses power. Read it with Wireshark (PacketLogger) or BTstack's tools/; Number of Completed Packets against the data packets shows the controller's buffer use, Disconnection Complete has the reason.

Cost (RP2350, Release, arm-none-eabi-size on neupod.elf, origin/main 701c8f2 against this change): text 1,411,808 to 1,415,144 B (+3,336 B), bss 499,876 to 499,948 B (+72 B: link statistics, the policy state, the encoder's saved settings). Free SRAM about 5.6 KB before, 72 B less now. The core-1 closure check is green (Release and Debug); nothing here is reachable from core 1, and the Y2's BTstack thread still makes no RTOS call (the HCI trace flusher is a plain pthread using fsync).

What to watch on the next walk. wait max and stalls in the bad patches (does the catch-up refill: catchup up to about 90 ms, drops near 0?); bitpool stepping and the time it spends below 53 (does the headset sound better at 45, and does it step back up); inflight against T; the rssi values on a good and a bad stretch; any acl down with its reason; and that no route: not playing ... suspending appears while playing.

docs.title: Stage 2c: AVRCP, volume, buttons, metadata (built)
docs.text:
Roles. The headset is the AVRCP target of absolute volume (category 2) and we are its controller for that; for the buttons and the display we are the target (category 1, player) and the headset is the controller. BTstack creates both roles on every AVRCP link, so MAX_NR_AVRCP_CONNECTIONS is 2 (640 B each) and the SDP records of both roles are registered (107 and 114 bytes). The headset normally opens the AVRCP channel itself (AirPods do); if it has not 2 s after the A2DP signalling channel we open it. The adapter (hal/common/bt_btstack/bt_btstack.c, same code on the RP2350 and the Y2) follows the verified y2-a2dp tool.

HAL (hal_radio.h, ADR-0019 section 1). HAL_BT_EVT_VOLUME (0..127), hal_bt_volume_set(), hal_bt_volume_supported() / hal_bt_volume_get(), HAL_BT_EVT_KEY (PLAY, PAUSE, PLAY_PAUSE, NEXT, PREV, STOP, FF, RW; presses only), hal_bt_track_info() (title, artist, album, duration, position, play status, track id; returns false when the stack is busy with the previous call, the app asks again at its next tick). "Absolute volume supported" means the headset has reported a volume on the AVRCP channel (the answer to our volume-change registration): it turns true a moment after CONNECTED and false when the channel or the link goes; a headset that rejects the registration never turns it true and the software volume stays. Our own volume commands are sent without waiting for each answer (BTstack allows several in flight), the latest value wins, and the headset's reports that cross our commands are ignored so the bar does not jump back. No FreeRTOS call is made on the BTstack thread (the Y2 rule of bt_port_stpbt.c): the track information is one copy under a try-lock that neither side waits on, events leave through bt_port_deliver().

Volume policy (app/runtime/bt_control.c). On the Bluetooth output with absolute volume the wheel moves the headset's volume (hal_bt_volume_set, 4 of 127 per step, 32 steps lock to lock), the software volume is held at 0 dB (player_volume_hold_unity; the user's software level is kept and comes back when the headset is not the volume), and a swipe on the stem moves the bar. Without absolute volume, or on the wired output, the software volume is the volume as before. One scale (bt_vol_to_db / bt_vol_from_db): 127 = 0 dB, 0 = the software "off" level (80 dB), linear in dB, so a wheel step is about 2 dB in both modes; host-tested. On connect the headset's volume is read and shown; no earlier level is ever restored to the headset. One exception, the owner's decision of 12 Nov 2026 ("cap it"): when the headset's first volume report on a connection is above 50 % (NEUPOD_BT_VOLUME_CAP_ON_CONNECT, 64 of 127, runtime_config.h), the player turns it down to 50 % before the software volume is released to 0 dB (bt: headset volume capped N% -> 50%). Only ever down, never up; a swipe or the wheel afterwards above 50 % is respected; each new connection is a new first report. Host-tested (bt_control). If it reports 0 the bar is empty, the label says Headset 0% and the status line says Playing - headset volume 0% (the AirPods Pro that a phone left at 0 % are no longer silently "playing"). Deviation: no per-headset volume is stored (asked as "if cheap"): the headset keeps its own level, which is the truth, and re-applying an old level behind the user's back is a loudness risk.

Buttons. Done by the monitor task, so they work with any screen open or none: Play/Pause toggle; PLAY only when not playing and PAUSE only when playing (a repeated or crossed press does no harm); STOP pauses (the place is kept; a later PLAY resumes); NEXT / PREV are Right / Left (a folder queue is needed, and Previous restarts a track more than 3 s in); FF / RW scrub by the Now Playing step (a 60th of the track, 1 to 30 s) per press, so holding the button repeats. A button press does not wake the backlight.

Track information. While a link exists the track's title (the file name without a title tag), artist, album, length, position and play status are handed over when the track or the status changes, when the position jumps more than 2 s (a seek), and every 10 s. The stack extrapolates the position while playing, answers the headset's play-status queries, and sends the track-changed and playback-status notifications. Nothing is sent for a test tone.

UI. Now Playing: Headset 62% and a bar on the same 0..127 scale; Test tone the same. Settings > Bluetooth pane: Absolute volume: yes / no (the pane no longer says On while a stream is open, to make room). Tours at 320x240 and 480x360: np-bt-volume, np-bt-volume0, bt-key-next (UI).

Memory (RP2350, Release): text 1,350,480 B to 1,374,856 B (+24,376 B, AVRCP, the volume / key / metadata policy and the reconnect policy, UI), bss 496,548 B to 498,596 B (+2,048 B: two AVRCP connections 1,280 B, SDP records 232 B, track information and state about 400 B), so free SRAM falls from about 7.7 KB to about 5.6 KB. The 6 KB worker stack now also runs the AVRCP code: its minimum is on the bench list. The core-1 closure check reports ok.

On the board (stage 2c), in this order.

  1. Y2, AirPods Pro, connected after the iPhone left them at 0 %: Now Playing shows Headset 0% and the hint; turn the wheel: sound, the bar follows; swipe the stem: the bar follows (console: bt: avrcp: headset volume N%).
  2. Press the stem / buttons: Play/Pause, double and triple press give Next / Previous. The track changes on the device; the headset display (if any) shows title and artist.
  3. A headset without absolute volume (a speaker): Absolute volume: no, the wheel is the software volume as before.
  4. The WI-C200 and the RP2350: the same, plus the worker stack minimum and the free SRAM.

docs.title: Reconnecting (stage 3, built)
docs.text: app/runtime/bt_reconnect.c (pure policy) driven by bt_service.c. After the link to the remembered headset is lost (HAL_BT_FAIL_LINK_LOST: out of range, switched off without saying goodbye) Connect is tried again after 2 s, 5 s, 10 s, then every 30 s, for 5 minutes in all. At power-up, once Bluetooth is on and the settings are loaded, one attempt is made at once and the same schedule follows if it fails. Every attempt is ended by the HAL's own connect timer (20 s; the MT6582 does not report its page timeout until the connection is cancelled). Any action of the user ends it for good (Disconnect, Forget, Pair, Connect, Cancel); a running scan or somebody else's Pair / Connect only holds it back. A headset that hangs up politely (idle disconnect, 0x13) is not "lost" and is not chased. The headset row reads Reconnecting... with busy dots from the loss until it is back, or given up. Playback is not resumed by a reconnect: the pause from the drop stays (Play, or the headset's button, continues). Not built: auto-resume of playback.

docs.title: Stage 2 design notes (2a, 2b and 2c built)
docs.text:
• Priority and RAM (ADR-0013, amendment of 4 Nov 2026): stage 2 follows the Audio Pack tone test and MP3/ALAC playback. The original funding (sizing the codec arena, releasing LVGL's second render buffer) no longer pays: the arena saving was already spent in #17, and free SRAM is now about 15 KB (15,320 B measured on main, 14,876 B with stage 2a). The core 1 to core 0 Bluetooth PCM ring reuses the 32 KB I2S PCM ring storage: the outputs are exclusive (I2S or Bluetooth, never both), so the same bytes serve whichever sink is active. That adds no new static RAM; the SBC encoder state and working buffers are measured in 2b and come out of the free SRAM.
  • Hi-res audio to Bluetooth: decimated on core 1 by a 2:1 or 4:1 half-band FIR to 44.1 / 48 kHz, with 24 to 16 bit TPDF dither, before the samples enter the core 1 to core 0 ring. SBC cannot carry more than 48 kHz / 16 bit.
  • Wi-Fi during A2DP: allowed (Stuart's decision, provisional, see Wi-Fi alongside Bluetooth: one policy macro, no interlock). The stage 2b bench test has to show an A2DP stream stable while Wi-Fi comes and goes.

  • Final board radio: not a bare CYW43439 (assembly and licence, ADR-0007); the stage 2 code stays behind hal_bt_*.

  • Verify while Wi-Fi toggles: the Wi-Fi service switches the station on and off (playback pause, idle timeout) on the same radio worker that runs BTstack. Before relying on it, check on the board that an A2DP stream stays stable (no dropouts, no HCI resets) when Wi-Fi comes and goes, and with "Wi-Fi while playing" On.

  • Pairing and saved device (2a, built): see above.

  • A2DP source: BTstack's a2dp_source with one SBC stream endpoint; SBC at 44.1 kHz, joint stereo, 16 blocks, 8 subbands, bitpool 53 (about 328 kbit/s) as the default and a high bitpool (SBC-XQ, up to what the headset's capabilities allow; the AirPods Pro 3 also offer AAC, which we do not do) when the sink accepts it. The encoder is pico_btstack_sbc_encoder (Bluedroid, Apache-2.0).
  • Audio routing: today core 1's decoder fills a PCM ring that its own I2S/null sink drains. For Bluetooth, a new core 1 to core 0 PCM ring (single producer, single consumer, the same spsc_ring rules, 16-bit stereo, roughly 150 to 250 ms) receives the decoded and volume-scaled samples; a core 0 "bt audio" task (or the BTstack worker itself) takes them, encodes SBC frames and hands media packets to BTstack. Core 1 gains a "virtual sink" mode (the null sink's hardware alarm timing) so the decoder keeps its block cadence; nothing on core 1 uses the RTOS, and the ring and its counters join the closure check.
  • Source-side pacing: a source must deliver samples at the sample rate, but the headset's clock is not ours. The ring is the buffer: the link's own flow control (the controller's ACL buffers, can send now events) slows the encoder task when the headset consumes slowly, the ring then fills, and the decoder on core 1 (which only decodes when the ring has room) slows with it, so the decoder is paced by the link. A fill-level target (about half the ring) with an occasional one-frame drop or repeat on drift keeps it steady; underruns on the Bluetooth path are counted like the I2S ones. To be proven on the bench with the AirPods Pro 3.
  • AVRCP (2c, built, above): the headset's absolute volume is the player's volume, play/pause/next/previous from the headset's buttons, and track metadata for the headset display.
  • UI (2a built: pairing flow, saved device and state in the pane): still to come, negotiated codec and battery (if the headset reports it) in the pane; the Now Playing badge shows the codec (UI).

docs.title: What to check on the board (stage 2a)
docs.text:
Only the hardware can confirm these; the host simulator and tests cover the state machine, the saved record and the UI.

  1. Pair. Headset in pairing mode (AirPods Pro 3: case open, button held until the light flashes white). Settings > Bluetooth > Scan for devices > Select the headset: busy dots, then "Paired, no audio yet" within a few seconds; UART shows bt: pair, bt: paired with, bt: connected to ... (A2DP sink found). Back on Settings > Bluetooth the headset is listed, the right pane shows its name and state.
  2. Never discoverable; connectable only while pairing, and only for the chosen headset. No phone ever sees "neuPod" in its Bluetooth list, before, during or after a Pair. During a Pair a second device (or the same phone) that tries to connect to neuPod by address is rejected, and no key is created for it; after Connected / Failed / Cancel nothing can connect.
  3. Link key on the card, not in flash. After pairing, /.neupod/settings.a or .b has changed and no other path on the card; reboot: the headset is still listed. Nothing writes the internal flash (core 1 and the audio underrun counter unaffected during the Pair; underruns=0).
  4. Connect / Disconnect / Forget. Disconnect, Connect: reaches Connected again with the stored key and without the headset being put in pairing mode (it must be on and not connected to something else). Forget (twice Select): the row disappears; Connect is gone; pair again works. Key lost on the headset side (forget neuPod in its own settings or factory reset it): Connect shows "Failed: pairing refused", it does not silently re-pair.
  5. Failures. Headset switched off: Connect shows "Failed: not found" within the 20 s limit. A phone as the target: "Failed: not a headset" and no saved device afterwards. Walk away from the headset until it drops: "Failed: link lost" (or "Not connected" if it closed an idle link). Menu on the Devices screen during a Pair cancels it.
  6. The idle link. (2a) The headset hung up after 1 to 2 s without a profile; since 2b the stream keeps the link up. Also: Connect with the key deleted from the card by hand fails at once with "pairing refused" and no radio traffic; and a headset that is busy with another phone during a Pair says "busy or not pairing".
  7. Wi-Fi alongside (provisional policy). With Wi-Fi joined and a transfer running, Pair, Connect and Disconnect: no HCI reset, no Wi-Fi drop, no stalled transfer. Also with "Wi-Fi while playing" On and a file playing from the card (I2S path, no Bluetooth audio yet): underruns=0.
  8. Memory. Monitor lines heap: free=... min_free=..., lvgl_mem, and the radio worker's stack minimum after several Pair / Connect / Forget cycles: the worker's free stack must stay clear of zero (the new code and its printfs run there).
  9. Repeat Pair 10 times (Forget in between) and with a headset that connects back to us by itself right after pairing (we are connectable during the Pair for this): no stuck "Pairing...", no orphan key (Forget leaves the card with no BTL record (tag "BTL" + raw slot number 0..7) for it).

docs.title: What to check on the board (stage 1)
docs.text:
1. Flash neupod.elf with the Pico 2 W, open the UART. Watch for the three bt: lines above after the splash, boot: bluetooth ok and boot: wifi DEGRADED. The splash should show Bluetooth solid and Wi-Fi with a cross (that is intended in stage 1).
  2. Audio must be unaffected: play a file while the radio comes up; the audio: line must keep underruns=0 and the core1_stack_free= value must not drop.
  3. Settings > Bluetooth: Status "On", the same address as the UART, Scan for devices (opens Devices and scans at once) with a headset in pairing mode (AirPods Pro 3: case open, button held until the light flashes white): it appears with a speaker symbol, a name after a few seconds and a signal value; other devices around you are greyed out. Select on it starts pairing (stage 2a; see its checklist above). Menu leaves and stops the scan.
  4. Change the backlight and Click feedback, switch the board off and on: both should come back. Change the volume to a quiet level and check it returns; set it loud and check it comes back at -30 dB. A /.neupod/settings.a (and later .b) should be on the card; no other file or folder on the card may have changed.
  5. Boot once without a card: the UART shows settings: no usable card ... and the screens still work.
  6. Read the monitor's heap: free=... min_free=... and lvgl_mem=.../... lines (and chk_radio / the worker's stack figure) after using every menu and one scan, and keep the minimums.

docs.title: Click-wheel protocol (iPod Classic 6G)
docs.text: Source: Rockbox ipod6g reverse-engineering (firmware/target/arm/s5l8702/, ipod/button-clickwheel.c) and the community 5G click-wheel teardown; see Design → Click wheel. Items marked TBC are unconfirmed on the 6G.

docs.title: Electrical
docs.text:
Line Direction Notes CLK wheel → host open-drain, ~53 kHz, generated by the wheel SDO wheel → host open-drain, frame data SDI host → wheel init packet 4th line TBC configured with the other three by the S5L8702; likely WAKE or enable
  • 18 kΩ pull-ups on CLK/SDO, located on the wheel's own flex (5G teardown; verify on the 6G with a meter before adding board pull-ups).
  • The wheel has its own 3.0 V LDO; 3.3 V from our board is fine.

docs.title: Frames (wheel → host)
docs.text:
The wheel streams 32-bit frames, LSB first.

A frame x is valid when:

(x & 0x800000FF) == 0x8000001A
Bits Field 0–7 0x1A (frame marker, part of the validity check) 8 Select 9 Right 10 Left 11 Play 12 Menu 16–22 Finger position, 0–95 (3.75° per count, clockwise, 0 at Menu) 30 Finger on wheel 31 1 (part of the validity check)

docs.title: Host → wheel
docs.text:
The host sends one init packet, 0x8000023A, at start-up and again after Hold is released. This is the only host transmission Rockbox makes. The wheel replies with a 0x8000023A-type frame carrying button state in bits 16–20. Its low byte is 0x3A, so the frame-validity check above rejects it.

On the S5L8702 the packet is written to the WHEEL peripheral's TX register (WHEELTX) and the hardware shifts it out.

docs.title: Hold
docs.text: On Hold, Rockbox stops the wheel controller and drives all four lines low as GPIO. On release it re-initialises the wheel and re-sends the init packet. neuPod should idle or power-gate the wheel the same way to save battery.

docs.title: Scrolling (Rockbox constants)
docs.text:
Constant Value Counts per revolution 96 Counts per list step 4 Untouched debounce 150 ms Repeat timeout 250 ms

These are Rockbox's UI tuning values, not protocol requirements.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Host → wheel init packet: not documented anywhere in the open. Plan (3 Nov 2026): capture all four wheel lines on the donor iPod with the logic analyser from power-on (Rockbox boot). That shows which side drives SDI/SDO, the clock source during the init packet, and its timing. Until then the UI is driven from the UART keys.

  • Mapping of the four lines to GP19/26/27/28 (see Phase 1 wiring); measure with a logic analyser on the donor's stock board.
  • Identity and function of the fourth line.
  • Which edge of CLK data is valid on, and how frame boundaries are delimited.
  • Whether the wheel or the host drives CLK while the init packet is sent.
  • Pull-up location on the 6G (assumed wheel flex, as on the 5G).

Firmware: app/include/clickwheel_frame.h (decoder), platforms/rp2350/hal/hal_input.c (PIO receiver), tests in tests/.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
Exported from the neuPod design doc (Design tab, 27 Oct – 1 Nov 2026). Companion to the Requirements. This page records the engineering decisions: architecture, pin budget, interfaces to the reused iPod parts, and what remains to be verified. Phase 1 target is a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W on the bench driving the donor's click wheel, LCD and headphone flex.

Decisions with lasting consequences are also recorded as ADRs.

docs.title: Goal and scope
docs.text:
Build the firmware and the replacement logic board in two phases:

  1. Phase 1 — bench testbed. A Pico 2 W on a breadboard with off-the-shelf breakouts (display, microSD, I²S DAC, fuel gauge, haptic driver) and, once measured and broken out, the donor's own click wheel and headphone/hold flex. Every driver written here must port unchanged to the final board through the HAL.
  2. Phase 2 — custom board. An RP2350B (or ESP32-S3) board to the mid-frame's outline, with the final display, DAC, charger and radio.

docs.title: Target hardware
docs.text: Block Phase 1 (bench) Final board Compute Pico 2 W (RP2350A, 26 GPIO, 4 MB flash, no PSRAM) RP2350B + 8 MB APS6404L PSRAM (QSPI CS1) + 16 MB W25Q128 flash Radio CYW43439 on Pico 2 W via internal SPI (uses GP23/24/25/29 — not available to us) Not a bare CYW43439; RM2 module or ESP32 — open (ADR-0007) Display Adafruit 2.0" 320×240 IPS TFT (ST7789) on SPI1, landscape — see wiring ER-TFT024IPS-3 (or RM690B0 AMOLED), 8080-16 via PIO if pins allow Storage microSD, SDIO 4-bit via PIO on GP2–7 (ADR-0006; SPI mode is the fallback) SDIO 4-bit Audio Pimoroni Pico Audio Pack: PCM5100A + PAM8908 (I²S on GP9–11, GP22 = XSMT, active low) ES8311 / ES8388 / PCM5102A, MCLK provided (ADR-0012) Input Donor click wheel via FPC breakout; hold switch from headphone flex Same Power USB from the Pico, Micro-Lipo (MCP73831) + MAX17048 for battery tests BQ25895 (0x6A) + fuel gauge, USB-C; SD VDD load switch USB Pico's native USB (TinyUSB: MSC + CDC) Native USB on USB-C

docs.title: Compute options
docs.text:
Available: GP0–GP22 and GP26–GP28 = 26 GPIO (GP23/24/25/29 are consumed by the wireless module). GP26–28 are the only ADC-capable pins.

Interface Signals Pins Notes LCD (SPI, 4-wire) SCK, MOSI, CS, DC, RST, backlight PWM 6 MISO omitted; ~19 fps full-frame at 62.5 MHz SPI, partial updates for UI. 8-bit 8080 (12–13 pins) does not fit on the 2 W alongside everything else microSD (SDIO 4-bit, PIO) CLK, CMD, D0–D3 6 Fallback: SPI mode on SPI0 with its own CS = 4 pins (D1/D2 become CD/unused) I²S audio BCLK, LRCLK, DOUT 3 PIO I²S; the PCM5100A needs no MCLK. Final board adds MCLK from clk_gpout (+1) I²C (shared bus) SDA, SCL 2 DAC control, fuel gauge, charger, haptic driver, future touch Click wheel Serial data, clock, enable/power, (optional extra) 3–4 Pinout and protocol to be confirmed from Rockbox s5l8702/ipod6g wheel driver and a logic-analyser capture of the stock board Headphone/hold flex Hold switch, headphone detect 2 Remote/accessory lines (2) left unconnected in Phase 1 Battery / power Thermistor (ADC), charger INT or PGOOD 2 Thermistor on GP26–28 Haptic (optional) Enable/trigger 1 DRV2605L on I²C Debug UART TX, RX 2 Optional — USB CDC can replace it once USB is up Total 27–28 with everything 24 with SD in SPI mode and no UART — fits. SDIO + no haptic + no UART = 25 — fits

Conclusion: the Pico 2 W works for Phase 1 if the LCD is SPI and either SD is SPI or haptics/UART are dropped. There is no headroom for a parallel LCD bus. The final board (RP2350B, 48 GPIO) lifts this: 8080-16 LCD (20 pins) + SDIO (6) + I²S with MCLK (4) + I²C (2) + wheel (4) + flex (4) + power (3) + haptic (1) + radio SPI (5 if CYW43439) ≈ 49 — so even the B variant is tight with a 16-bit bus; 8080-8 (12 pins) is the likely final choice.

The application layer (LVGL UI, FatFs, codecs, library logic) is portable C. What is not portable is the radio and USB stack, and two requirements constrain the chip: classic Bluetooth A2DP (AirPods, most headphones) and USB mass storage.

Chip A2DP source Native USB device Verdict RP2350 + CYW43439 Yes (BTstack; Sprout) Yes Current plan; 150 MHz M33 + PIO is enough ESP32 (original, WROVER-E) Yes (ESP-IDF / ESP-ADF) No Strong audio stack, 240 MHz, PSRAM; needs Wi-Fi-only transfer or a USB-SD bridge/mux ESP32-S3 No (BLE only) Yes Best MCU on paper; needs an external A2DP transmitter ESP32-P4 + C6 No Yes Overkill; C6 is BLE only STM32H7 / nRF / i.MX RT No radio Yes External Wi-Fi/BT module either way

Escape hatch: a dedicated Bluetooth audio transmitter IC/module on I²S (Qualcomm QCC30xx/QCC51xx, Microchip BM83, BK3266-class) removes the A2DP constraint, adds aptX/LDAC, and makes the ESP32-S3 the strongest alternative. Decision: RP2350 + CYW43439 for Phase 1; keep the radio behind an interface so the ESP32-S3 + external A2DP route stays open for the final board.

docs.title: Connectivity
docs.text:
Effect of an external Bluetooth audio module (Qualcomm QCC3008/3040/5125, Microchip BM83): A2DP and codec negotiation (AAC, aptX HD, some LDAC) move off the MCU; it streams I²S and controls the module over UART. That removes the RP2350's main advantage (BTstack A2DP) and makes the ESP32-S3 the better host (240 MHz, octal PSRAM, native USB, hardware QSPI for the AMOLED, ESP-ADF).

A: RP2350 + CYW43439 B: ESP32-S3 + QCC module C: RP2350 + QCC module BT codecs SBC / SBC-XQ AAC, aptX HD, (LDAC) AAC, aptX HD, (LDAC) Wi-Fi CYW43439 On-chip CYW43439 AMOLED QSPI PIO, reduced fps Native peripheral PIO, reduced fps Extra parts None QCC module + antenna QCC module + CYW43439 (two radios) Firmware Pico SDK + BTstack ESP-IDF + ESP-ADF Pico SDK, no BT stack Power Lowest Moderate Moderate

Bench test to decide: Pico 2 W running BTstack SBC-XQ vs a QCC3008 transmitter board (~£8, AliExpress/eBay) or BM83 eval module fed from the Audio Pack, both paired to AirPods.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: microSD over SDIO 4-bit on PIO (GP2–GP7 on the testbed), FatFs with exFAT, cards up to 2 TB. SPI mode is the fallback (CLK = SCK, CMD = MOSI, DAT0 = MISO, DAT3 = CS), which frees two GPIOs for the hold switch and headphone detect on the Pico 2 W. The card and the display sit on different buses so a frame refresh and an audio-buffer fill can run concurrently on DMA. See Requirements → Storage.

docs.title: Display
docs.text: Phase 1 uses the Adafruit 2.0" 320×240 IPS TFT (ST7789) on SPI1 in landscape — see ADR-0002 and the wiring page. The final-board candidates (EastRising ER-TFT024IPS-3 and the 2.4" RM690B0 AMOLED) are in Requirements → Display.

docs.title: Stock LCD (plan B only)
docs.text: Item Value Source Bus 8080-series parallel, 18-bit data bus physically (D0–D17) plus CS, RS/DC, WR, RD, RESET, TE (tearing-effect) and a 2-bit panel ID lcd-s5l8702.c Pixel transfers RGB565, one transfer per pixel, on D[17:10] + D[8:1] ("Type II" 16-bit wiring — D0 and D9 unused for data) lcd-s5l8702.c Panel types Four supplier variants, read from GPIO 6.4/6.5 at boot. Types 0 and 1: 8-bit MIPI-DCS command set (ILI9340-like) on D[8:1] — 0x2A/0x2B window, 0x2C memory write, 0x11/0x29 wake, 0x28/0x10 sleep, 0x3A=0x06 18-bit pixel format, 0x35 TE on. Types 2 and 3: 16-bit register set (ILI9320/9326-like) — 0x200/0x201 GRAM address, 0x202 write, 0x210–0x213 window; full init and gamma tables are in lcd-6g.c lcd-6g.c Timing Rockbox sets LCD_PHTIME 0x11 for normal, 0x33 for ID reads — i.e. a slow bus is tolerated; PIO can meet it easily lcd-s5l8702.c Backlight White-LED string driven by the PMU's boost LED driver (regs 0x28 brightness, 0x29 on/off, 0x2A OCP 500 mA, 0x2B dim step). Needs a boost LED driver on our board; string voltage to measure backlight-6g.c Pin cost ≥ 22 GPIO — rules it out on the Pico 2 W; viable only on the RP2350B board with an 8-bit command path and PIO — Connector FPC pin count/pitch to measure; ID pins must be read to pick the init sequence measure

docs.title: Stock audio codec (reference for the DAC choice)
docs.text:
Stock part is a Cirrus CS42L55 at I²C address 0x94 (8-bit), I²S from the SoC, reset on GPIO 3.3, master clock from the SoC (CLKCON3), analogue rail "Vcodec" 1.8 V from PMU LDO3 (2.4 V when recording). The CS43131 (its DAC-only successor) was the original plan; it is dropped for stock reasons, see ADR-0012.

The audio quality policy, the Bluetooth codec table and the recording requirement are in Requirements → Audio and ADR-0003.

docs.title: Stock power, battery and charging (reference)
docs.text: Item Stock Our equivalent PMU NXP PCF50635 ("D1671"): LDOs, backlight boost, ADC, hold/EXTON inputs, standby/wake Discrete: buck + LDOs, LED boost, fuel gauge Charger LTC4066 with HPWR (100/500 mA), SUSP, CLPROG (current doubling) GPIOs; battery charge limited to ~330–340 mA by RPROG BQ25895/BQ24074 with power-path; set charge current for the chosen cell Battery sense PMU ADC BATSNS, 10-bit, averaged Fuel gauge (BQ27441/MAX17048) or ADC divider Battery connector 3-pin (cell+, thermistor, cell−) to measure pitch Same, or JST for a raw cell USB D+/D− routed to PMU ADC to detect charger type; USB insert on GPIO 12.3 Native USB; CC pulldowns FireWire/dock power PMU EXTON input Not needed Storage 1.8" ATA over 40-pin ZIF, power-gated via PMU microSD Dock accessory serial UART on the 30-pin (iPod Accessory Protocol) + accessory-ID resistor via PMU ADC Dropped (USB-C replaces the dock)

docs.title: Phase 1 power rails
docs.text:
• Bench power: Pico's USB-C (VBUS 5 V) → VSYS → on-board buck-boost → 3V3. Budget on 3V3: SD ~100 mA peak, Audio Pack ~50 mA, I²C boards <5 mA, CYW43439 up to ~300 mA bursts. Keep the TFT on VSYS.
  • Battery test: LiPo → MAX17048 → Micro-Lipo charger (charges from the charger's own USB-C) → Schottky → VSYS. With both USBs plugged in, the Pico runs from whichever is higher; the diode keeps them apart.
  • All grounds common; star them at the Pico GND pins.

docs.title: Reused parts and mechanical
docs.text: Source: Rockbox git, firmware/target/arm/s5l8702/ (lcd-s5l8702.c, ipod6g/lcd-6g.c, ipod/button-clickwheel.c, ipod6g/pmu-6g.c, backlight-6g.c, cscodec-6g.c, mikey-6g.c, power-6g.c, adc-6g.c), plus the community 5G click-wheel teardown for the physical layer. What follows is what our board must replicate for each reused part; items marked measure still need the donor.

docs.title: Click wheel
docs.text:
The wheel is a self-contained touch controller (a Cypress PSoC on the 5G; same protocol family on the 6G) that streams 32-bit frames to the host. The S5L8702 uses a dedicated "WHEEL" peripheral on four port-14 pins (PCON14 bits 8–23, alt-function 2); on our board this is a PIO state machine or a GPIO interrupt.

Item Value Source Lines to the host CLK (wheel → host, open-drain, ~53 kHz), SDO (wheel → host, open-drain), SDI (host → wheel), plus a 4th line the SoC configures with the other three — likely WAKE or enable. 18 kΩ pull-ups on the 5G flex 5G teardown; Rockbox PCON14 4-pin config Supply Wheel has its own LDO (3.0 V out); fed from the iPod system rail (3.3–4.2 V). 3.3 V from our board is fine 5G teardown Frame 32 bits, LSB first, clocked by the wheel. Valid frame: (status & 0x800000FF) == 0x8000001A. Bits 8–12 = Select, Right, Left, Play, Menu (1 = pressed). Bits 16–22 = finger position 0–95 (3.75°/count, clockwise, 0 at Menu). Bit 30 = finger on wheel. Bit 31 always set Rockbox button-clickwheel.c Host → wheel On init and after Hold is released the host sends 0x8000023A; the wheel replies with a 0x8000023A-type frame carrying button state in bits 16–20. That is the only host transmission Rockbox makes Rockbox s5l_clickwheel_init() Hold behaviour On Hold, Rockbox stops the wheel controller and drives the 4 lines as GPIO (low); on release it re-inits. We should power-gate or idle the wheel the same way for battery life Rockbox button_read_device() Scroll handling 96 counts/rev; Rockbox uses 4 counts per list step, velocity-based acceleration, 150 ms "untouched" debounce, 250 ms repeat timeout. Reuse these constants Rockbox Connector 5G: 13-pin 0.3 mm FPC (DDK FF12-13A-R11AL-3H). 6G Classic: pin count and pitch to measure on the donor 5G teardown; measure Phase 1 plan Breakout the FPC; probe CLK/SDO on the stock board with a logic analyser to confirm which 6G pins are CLK, SDO, SDI and the 4th line; then PIO receiver on the Pico —

docs.title: Headphone / hold-switch flex
docs.text: Item Value Source Hold switch Not on a SoC GPIO: it goes to the PMU's GPIO2 (PCF50635 GPIOSTAT) with an interrupt. On our board: plain GPIO with pull-up, active-low = locked pmu-6g.c, button_hold() Headphone detect SoC GPIO 10.6, high when a plug is inserted headphones_inserted() Inline remote / mic ("Mikey") The flex carries an I²C-controlled chip at address 0x72 that handles mic bias, Apple inline-remote volume/centre buttons and accessory ID. Needs I²C (shared bus) + mic bias from the codec rail. Register map is in mikey-6g.c (reg0 mode 0x2F = remote mode; reg4 centre button; reg5 vol ± events). Optional for us, but it means the flex has SDA/SCL on it mikey-6g.c Audio lines L, R, GND from the codec's headphone amp; mic line to Mikey — Connector ZIF; pin count/pitch to measure measure

docs.title: What this means for the Phase 1 harness
docs.text:
1. Click wheel: 4 lines + 3.3 V + GND. Pull-ups to 3.3 V on CLK/SDO (18 kΩ). PIO clocked-serial receiver; one GPIO for the host init packet.
  2. Hold + headphone detect: two GPIO inputs with pull-ups.
  3. I²C bus: Mikey (0x72) on the headphone flex if we want the inline remote; CS43131 and the fuel gauge later.
  4. Stock LCD: skip on the Pico 2 W. Use the Adafruit 2.0" ST7789 over SPI1 (the ER-TFT024IPS-3 is the final-board candidate).
  5. No change to the earlier pin budget except the wheel is confirmed as 4 lines, not 3.

docs.title: Development environments
docs.text:
Layer Environment What runs there Application (UI, library index, playback logic, codecs, FatFs) Host-native build (PICO_PLATFORM=host, LVGL SDL backend, FatFs on a disk-image file, SDL audio) Day-to-day development and unit tests; wheel mapped to mouse/keys Drivers (ST7789 SPI/PIO, click-wheel PIO receiver, SD, I²C) Wokwi (RP2350 / Pico 2 simulation with PIO, SPI, I²C, ST7789 part); Renode as RP2350 support matures Driver bring-up before hardware; scripted wheel-frame injection Radio, USB, audio, power Pico 2 W + Debug Probe, then the custom board BTstack A2DP, CYW43439, TinyUSB, I²S/DAC, charger/fuel gauge — no useful emulation

Repo layout to support this: app/ (portable C), hal/host/ and hal/rp2350/, tests/ (host), tools/ (PC-side sync/updater, C# welcome here).

Project name: neuPod. Firmware repo at ~/projects/neuPod on the bench Linux box (SDK and tools shared under ~/pico: pico-sdk ≥ 2.1, pico-extras, pico-playground, picotool, OpenOCD with CMSIS-DAP). Build with PICO_BOARD=pico2_w, PICO_PLATFORM=rp2350-arm-s; flash over the Debug Probe with OpenOCD; UART console via the Probe at 115200. Editing via VS Code Remote-SSH + Claude Code on the box.

docs.title: Project layout
docs.text: The firmware repo is this repository (~/projects/neuPod on the bench Linux box). SDK and tools are shared under ~/pico: pico-sdk ≥ 2.1, pico-extras, pico-playground, picotool, OpenOCD with CMSIS-DAP. Build with PICO_BOARD=pico2_w, PICO_PLATFORM=rp2350-arm-s; flash over the Debug Probe with OpenOCD; UART console via the Probe at 115200. Layout: app/ (portable C), hal/include/ (HAL headers), platforms/rp2350/, platforms/esp32s3/, hal/host/ (SDL build), tests/, tools/, boards/. See ADR-0005.

docs.text: The parts and prototype-spin estimates are in Requirements → Cost; the supplier list is on the Reference page.

docs.text: See Requirements → Prior art. The Rockbox ipod6g target is the primary source for every reused-part interface on this page.

docs.text:

docs.title: Questions raised at export (1 Nov 2026)
docs.text:
Click wheel

  • [ ] Mapping of CLK / SDO / SDI / 4th line to GP19 / GP26 / GP27 / GP28: not yet measured. The design doc's working assumption is GP19 = CLK, GP26 = SDO, GP27 = SDI, GP28 = 4th line, chosen only so the PIO receiver can use a contiguous pin pair; the wiring page correctly keeps all four as TBC until the donor's stock board is probed with the logic analyser.
  • [ ] What the 4th line is: Rockbox configures four port-14 pins together for the S5L8702's WHEEL peripheral; the 5G teardown names SDI, SDO, CLK plus WAKE and RESET outputs. The 4th line is probably WAKE or an enable, unconfirmed.
  • [ ] Data sample edge and frame delimiting: not in any source we hold. Capture CLK/SDO with the logic analyser and read it off the trace. Frames are 32 bits LSB-first; the validity test (x & 0x800000FF) == 0x8000001A is the only framing Rockbox relies on.
  • [ ] How the host clocks out 0x8000023A: Rockbox writes it to the WHEEL peripheral's TX register (WHEELTX) and lets the hardware shift it; whether the wheel or the host drives CLK during that transfer is unknown — observe on the stock board.
  • [x] Where the 18 kΩ pull-ups sit: on the wheel's own flex (5G teardown). Treat the 6G the same but verify with a meter before adding board pull-ups.
  • [x] Added to click-wheel-protocol.md (1 Nov 2026), marked as Rockbox-sourced: after the init packet the wheel answers with a 0x8000023A-type frame carrying button state in bits 16–20; Rockbox's scroll constants (96 counts/rev, 4 counts per list step, 150 ms untouched debounce, 250 ms repeat timeout); Hold handling (stop the controller, drive the four lines low, re-init on release).

ST7789 (Adafruit 2.0" IPS, Phase 1)

  • [x] Confirmed on the bench 2026-11-02: MADCTL 0x60 (landscape), RGB order, offsets 0/0, INVON needed, backlight active high; SPI1 at 62.5 MHz (clk_sys 125 MHz) is clean. See display tests.

ESP32-S3 comparison module

  • [ ] Proposed, not yet decided: a module with 16 MB flash and 8 MB octal PSRAM (ESP32-S3-WROOM-1-N16R8 class dev board). Status LED: depends on the board chosen — record once bought. The S3 has BLE only, no classic Bluetooth, so A2DP on that path requires the external QCC module (see Connectivity).

Prior art

  • [x] Sprout: by certain things, London (Sean — seanpod on GitHub). Crowd Supply pre-launch page: https://www.crowdsupply.com/certain-things/sprout-pi-mainboard; studio page: https://certainthings.studio/sprout/.

docs.title: Phase 1 testbed wiring
docs.text:
Note

wiring-phase1.md is the source of truth for the pin plan. The tables below agree with it and add the breakout-module detail; the one difference is that the design doc proposed a tentative click-wheel line order, which is not adopted until the donor is measured (see Open items).

Everything runs at 3.3 V logic from the Pico's USB; the only exception is the TFT's Vin, which takes VSYS (5 V on USB) so its backlight boost doesn't load the Pico's 3V3 rail. The Audio Pack's fixed I²S pins (GP9–11, mute GP22) forced the SD block down to GP2–7 and I²C to GP20/21.

[embedded content: Phase 1 testbed · Pico 2 W and six modules, pins and buses]

Left column: debug, storage and power. Right column: display, audio and the I²C sensor chain. Every signal is 3.3 V; the TFT alone takes VSYS for its backlight supply.

docs.title: Display bring-up tests
docs.text: An interactive test menu for the Phase 1 display (Adafruit 2.0" 320x240 IPS TFT, ST7789, SPI1). The menu runs on the Pico and is driven from the PC's serial console: you type the keys on the PC, not on the Pico.

docs.title: Confirmed hardware settings
docs.text:
Confirmed on the bench (2026-11-02):

Setting Value Orientation / colour order MADCTL 0x60 (MX + MV, landscape), RGB order Inversion INVON (the panel needs it) Backlight GP8 PWM, active high System clock clk_sys = clk_peri = 125 MHz SPI1 62.5 MHz exactly (clk_peri / 2), 16-bit frames, DMA Console UART0 GP0/GP1, 115200 8N1 Column/row offset 0 / 0 (test 3 border visible on all four edges)

Measured on the bench (2026-11-02), all eight tests passing visual checks:

Measurement Result Full-screen blit from flash (test 5) 22 ms Same image via strip renderer (test 5) 23 ms Strip-rendered animation (test 7) 46.05 fps, 7.07 MB/s — 90 % of the 7.81 MB/s / 50.8 fps ceiling Random shapes (test 4) 91 strip-rendered frames in 2012 ms

docs.title: Build, flash, run
docs.text:
export PICO_SDK_PATH=$HOME/pico/pico-sdk
scripts/build.sh rp2350
scripts/flash.sh rp2350 display_test
scripts/console.sh          # minicom on the Debug Probe UART; type the keys here

Reset the board with the console already open to see the start-up line that reports clk_sys, clk_peri and the real SPI baud rate. On the PC, scripts/build.sh host builds the same menu as build/host/hal/host/display_test (keys from the terminal; with SDL installed it shows a window, otherwise set NEUPOD_DISPLAY_PPM=out.ppm to capture each frame). The Now Playing screen alone: build/host/hal/host/now_playing [8|16] [light].

docs.title: Menu keys
docs.text:
Key Action 1-8 Run that test a Run all, about 3 s each q Stop the running test and return to the menu b Toggle BGR order (MADCTL bit 3) i Toggle inversion r Cycle rotation: MADCTL 0x60, 0xA0, 0xE0, 0x20 m Print MADCTL and inversion state p Corner pattern: red top-left, green top-right, blue bottom-left, white bottom-right h / Enter Reprint the menu

b, i and r also work while a test is showing a static screen. Each test prints a VISUAL CHECK: line describing what you should see; if a display call fails it prints FAIL instead of relying on your eyes.

docs.title: Tests and what to look for
docs.text: # Test Should look like 1 Backlight White screen fades dark, full, dark over 4 s with no flicker or steps, then holds at 10 %, 50 %, 100 % 2 Colours Red, green, blue, white, black fills, uniform; 8 bars white-yellow-cyan-green-magenta-red-blue-black; four 256-step gradients. RGB565 has only 32/64/32 levels, so visible steps are expected 3 Sharpness 1-px checkerboard and gratings crisp; 1-px white border with all four edges visible; centred crosshair 4 Geometry Random lines, rectangles and circles (round, not oval), then a 32 x 24 grid of square cells 5 Image Same picture twice (one DMA from flash, then strip-rendered): arrow points right, yellow mark top-left, magenta top-right 6 Text Both fonts legible; Now Playing screen white-on-black then black-on-white in both fonts 7 Animation Bouncing ball with fading trail; prints fps and SPI MB/s against the 7.81 MB/s ceiling at 62.5 MHz 8 Sleep Image goes blank for 2 s, then returns without being redrawn

docs.title: Failure checklist
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause / action Image mirrored or rotated (test 5 arrow not pointing right, corner pattern in wrong corners) Wrong MADCTL orientation bits. Press r; confirmed value is 0x60 Red and blue swapped (red fill looks blue; yellow mark looks cyan) BGR bit. Press b Negative colours (white fill is black, red looks cyan) Inversion. Press i; the panel needs inversion on Smearing, noise, random pixels or grey haze on the 1-px gratings (test 3) SPI too fast for the wiring: shorten wires, add ground, or lower the SPI rate Garbage or horizontally shifted image, commands appearing as pixels D/C or CS timing: check GP16 (D/C) and GP13 (CS) wiring and that nothing else drives them Border line missing on one edge, or wrapped to the opposite side Column/row offset (TFT_COL_OFFSET / TFT_ROW_OFFSET) Backlight brightest at 0 and dark at 255 Backlight polarity inverted (it is active high on this board) Backlight never changes GP8 wiring, or PWM not attached to the backlight pin Blank or white after wake (test 8) Sleep/wake timing; the ST7789 should keep its frame memory in sleep Test 7 well below ~46 fps (measured) / 50.8 fps raw ceiling Clock not 125 MHz or SPI below 62.5 MHz: check the start-up line

docs.title: Source layout
docs.text: The tests live in app/tests/display_tests.c and use the portable drawing layer in app/gfx/ (primitives, two bitmap fonts, a strip renderer that draws 320x16 strips into two 10 KB buffers while DMA sends the previous one). Fonts: app/gfx/fonts/README.md. Images: tools/README.md. Pixels are native-endian RGB565 everywhere, matching the driver's 16-bit SPI frames.

docs.title: I2C peripherals: fuel gauge and haptics
docs.text:
Phase 1 breadboard: one I2C bus, I2C0 on the Pico 2 W, SDA = GP20, SCL = GP21, 400 kHz (fall back to 100 kHz if NACKs appear). Both breakouts carry their own pull-ups, so the firmware keeps the RP2350 internal pull-ups off (the pad reset state is pull-down enabled, so they are switched off explicitly). See Phase 1 wiring.

Device Board Address HAL Driver MAX17048 fuel gauge Adafruit MAX17048 0x36 hal_battery.h app/drivers/max17048.c DRV2605L haptic driver Adafruit DRV2605L 0x5A hal_haptic.h app/drivers/drv2605l.c

hal_power.h is kept for sleep and power-state control only; its old battery snapshot was never implemented and is replaced by hal_battery.h.

docs.title: Bus layer (hal_i2c.h)
docs.text:
• Every call is bounded: timeout = 2 x the byte time at the actual baud, never below 2 ms.
  • A NACK is a normal answer and never causes recovery. Only a timeout, or a line that is still low 100 us after a failed transfer, starts recovery: reset the controller, then (if SDA/SCL is low) switch the pins to GPIO, clock up to 9 SCL pulses (drive low / release, never drive high), generate a STOP and restore the I2C function. hal_i2c_get_stats() counts errors and recoveries.
  • Probing uses a 1-byte read (a zero-length write is unreliable on the RP2040/RP2350 controller) and skips the reserved ranges 0x00-0x07 and 0x78-0x7F.
  • Arbitration loss cannot be detected on the RP2350: the SDK clears the abort-source register before the HAL can read it, so ARB_LOST is never reported there. A lost arbitration that leaves a line low shows up as a stuck bus.
  • Reserved addresses are refused (BAD_PARAM) by every call, not just probes.
  • Dropping from 400 to 100 kHz is never automatic: hal_i2c_set_baud() is called by the test (or application) deliberately.

docs.title: MAX17048 (0x36)
docs.text:
Registers are 16-bit big-endian. Used here:

Reg Name Scaling / use 0x02 VCELL 78.125 uV per LSB (mV = raw x 5 / 64, rounded) 0x04 SOC 1/256 % per LSB (high byte = whole percent) 0x06 MODE bit 14 = quick-start 0x08 VERSION reads 0x001X 0x0A HIBRT high byte hibernate threshold 0.208 %/h per LSB, low byte active threshold 1.25 mV per LSB 0x0C CONFIG high byte RCOMP; low byte SLEEP (b7), ALSC (b6), ALRT (b5), ATHD (b4:0): alert at 32 - ATHD % 0x16 CRATE signed, 0.208 %/h per LSB 0x1A STATUS RI b8, VH b9, VL b10, VR b11, HD b12, SC b13, ENVR b14 0xFE CMD 0x5400 = power-on reset (the chip may NACK the write as it resets)

hal_battery_init() also clears STATUS.RI (power-up/reset indicator) so a later RI means a fresh reset; hal_battery_reset() waits 250 ms after the reset command and leaves RI set. Quick-start is only valid with no load on the cell. HIBRT as read from the bench chip: 0x8030 (observed, not asserted by the tests).

The driver uses integers only: millivolts, SOC in 1/256 %, rate in milli-percent per hour. A cell below 2.5 V counts as "no battery".

Source check

The MAX17048 scaling above comes from the Maxim/Analog Devices register descriptions as recalled when writing the driver; the datasheet PDF could not be downloaded in the build environment, so it is not yet cross-checked line by line. Check VCELL against a multimeter on the cell during bench test 2.

Bench note: the gauge is powered from the battery side. With no LiPo, or with a flat one, 0x36 disappears from the bus (a flat LiPo made 0x36 vanish on the bench). That is expected, not a wiring fault.

docs.title: DRV2605L (0x5A)
docs.text:
Checked against TI datasheet SLOS854D. Used here:

Reg Name Use 0x00 STATUS b7:5 DEVICE_ID (7 = DRV2605L), b3 DIAG_RESULT (1 = calibration failed; clears on read) 0x01 MODE b7 reset, b6 standby, b2:0: 0 internal trigger, 5 RTP, 7 auto-calibration 0x02 RTP_INPUT real-time amplitude 0x03 LIBRARY 1-5 and 7 ERM libraries A-F, 6 LRA 0x04-0x0B WAVEFORM_SEQ effect id 1-123, or bit 7 set = wait (n x 10 ms); 0 ends the sequence 0x0C GO start (clears itself at the end of playback / calibration) 0x16 / 0x17 RATED_VOLTAGE / OD_CLAMP see below 0x18 / 0x19 A_CAL_COMP / A_CAL_BEMF calibration results 0x1A FEEDBACK_CONTROL b7 ERM(0)/LRA(1), b6:4 brake factor, b3:2 loop gain, b1:0 BEMF gain 0x1B-0x1E CONTROL1-4 drive time, sample/blanking/idiss, ERM open-loop and RTP format, auto-cal time

docs.title: Motor
docs.text:
Adafruit 1201 "Vibrating Mini Motor Disc": ERM, 10 mm coin, brushed, rated 3.0 V (operates 2-5 V), about 11,000 rpm, about 75-100 mA running. Default drive mode is ERM open loop with ROM library 2 (TS2200 library B); the voltage ceiling is 3.6 V. Build-time defaults: NEUPOD_HAPTIC_ACTUATOR=HAL_HAPTIC_ERM and NEUPOD_HAPTIC_ERM_LOOP=HAL_HAPTIC_LOOP_OPEN (or HAL_HAPTIC_LOOP_CLOSED). Test menu keys: o toggles open/closed loop, e / l select ERM / LRA.

Why open loop: on the bench the closed-loop auto-calibration did not converge on this motor (3.0 V rated, 3.3 V supply; DIAG_RESULT failed after 1844 ms) and the motor buzzed instead of clicking. By user decision the ERM now runs open loop, which is also how Adafruit's own library drives this motor. Closed loop stays available (o key or build flag) for later experiments. The LRA path (library 6, LRA bit) is selectable at run time (Settings > Haptics > Actuator) and described below.

docs.title: LRA: LEADER LD0832AA
docs.text:
Target actuator for the final board: 8 mm coin LRA, rated 2.0 V rms, resonance about 235 Hz (build defaults in HAL_HAPTIC_LRA_LD0832AA, hal_haptic_lra_params_t; override at run time with hal_haptic_set_lra_params()). Not confirmed from the LCSC datasheet (C2682305): the datasheet could not be fetched from the build host, so 2.0 V rms and 235 Hz are the figures from the brief. Everything below is computed from those two numbers, so a different actuator only needs different parameters. The peak ceiling (2.8 V, 2 V x sqrt(2) floored) is a design choice, not a datasheet figure.

Value Formula (datasheet SLOS854D) Result LIBRARY LRA library 6 FEEDBACK N_ERM_LRA = 1, brake factor 2, loop gain 2, BEMF gain 2 (calibration overwrites the gain) 0xAA RATED_VOLTAGE Eq. 5: V rms = 20.58 mV x RV / sqrt(1 - (4 x tSAMPLE + 300 us) x f), tSAMPLE = 300 us, so RV = floor(2000 x sqrt(1 - 1500 us x 235) / 20.58) 78 (0x4E) OD_CLAMP Eq. 9: V peak = 21.22 mV x OD, so OD = floor(2800 / 21.22) 131 (0x83) = 2.78 V CONTROL1 STARTUP_BOOST + DRIVE_TIME = (half period - 0.5 ms) / 0.1 ms; half period 2.128 ms 0x90 (2.1 ms) CONTROL2 SAMPLE_TIME 3, BLANKING 1, IDISS 1 (datasheet defaults) 0xF5 CONTROL3 ERM_OPEN_LOOP and LRA_OPEN_LOOP cleared (closed loop, auto-resonance), RTP signed 0x80 CONTROL4 AUTO_CAL_TIME = 3 0x30

Click effect on an LRA: library 6 effect 4, Sharp Click 100 % (ERM keeps effect 3).

docs.title: Calibration and persistence
docs.text:
hal_haptic_calibrate() follows datasheet 8.5.6: MODE = 7, write the inputs above, GO, poll GO every 10 ms (through the delay hook, drv2605l_set_delay_fn; the firmware installs the scheduler delay so other tasks run), read STATUS DIAG_RESULT (1 = failed), then A_CAL_COMP, A_CAL_BEMF and BEMF_GAIN. A failure or timeout rebuilds the chip from reset with the previous good values.

The haptic task (core 0) owns this. The results are stored in the settings store (NPhc, 9 bytes: version, actuator, comp, bemf, gain, rated mV, peak mV, resonance Hz; version 2, 11 bytes) and re-applied on every boot, so the motor spins for the calibration once per actuator. It runs automatically when an LRA is selected (or built in) and no matching record exists, once the settings are known (the card's values have loaded, or there is no working card; a boot without a card cannot store it, so it repeats each boot). If the record cannot be stored (store full) the row shows Failed and a console line says so, and on demand from Settings > Haptics > Calibrate. Changing the actuator type, or the rated voltage, peak voltage or resonance (OD_CLAMP is a calibration input), makes the stored record not match, so it recalibrates (as does an old version 1 record, which had no peak); switching back and forth between types re-runs it for each. The task holds the I2C bus (the gauge read waits) for about a second but sleeps between polls, never blocking the UI. Clicks during it: rt_haptic_click() drops the request while the state is RUNNING (nothing is queued), and the task drains its queue when a calibration starts and again when it ends, which also discards a click that raced past the check. If the automatic attempt fails it is not retried until the next boot or a manual Calibrate.

docs.title: Click setting and rate limit
docs.text: Settings > Click: Piezo / Haptic / Both / Off (NPck 2 / 1 / 3 / 0). There is no piezo driver yet (NEUPOD_PIEZO_FITTED is 0), so the menu cycles Haptic / Off only; a Piezo or Both value already stored is accepted but silent (rt_piezo_click() is a stub). Haptic clicks go through a 2-deep queue and a 35 ms gate (haptic_gate_pass): a fast wheel spin drops requests instead of queueing them.

docs.title: Bring-up order (motor safety)
docs.text: In open loop OD_CLAMP is the full-scale drive (21.59 mV x OD, datasheet Eq. 6), so the clamp value must always match the loop mode in effect: 182 (the closed-loop value) would be about 3.93 V in open loop. The chip powers up open-loop. The driver therefore leaves standby, sets the chosen loop bit in CONTROL3 and reads it back, writes the feedback/timing registers, and writes RATED_VOLTAGE then OD_CLAMP last. If any step fails the chip is put back into standby and play/click/RTP/calibrate return an error until init succeeds. A failed or timed-out calibration resets the chip and re-applies the previous good calibration. The test menu puts the driver in a safe state (RTP 0, GO 0, standby) as soon as the bus comes up, and back in standby after every haptic test. The l (LRA) key is disabled unless the test is built with NEUPOD_I2C_TEST_ALLOW_LRA.

docs.title: Register values: ERM open loop (default)
docs.text:
Value Formula (datasheet Eq. 6) Result CONTROL3 ERM_OPEN_LOOP = 1 (power-on default), RTP signed 0xA0 OD_CLAMP V = 21.59 mV x OD, so OD = floor(3600 / 21.59) 166 (0xA6) = 3.584 V (167 would be 3.605 V) RATED_VOLTAGE ignored in open loop (datasheet 8.5.2.1); the closed-loop value is written as a safe one 141 (0x8D)

The datasheet constant is 21.59 mV per step for ERM open loop (Eq. 6), not 21.96 mV; the maximum open-loop clamp is therefore 166, enforced by the tests. Open-loop RTP is signed: 0 = no drive, 127 = +OD_CLAMP, negative values drive in reverse (braking). The ramp test only uses 0 to 127 to 0.

docs.title: Register values: ERM closed loop (optional, datasheet default timings)
docs.text:
Timings used: DRIVE_TIME = 0x13 (ERM: 1 ms + 19 x 0.2 ms = 4.8 ms), BLANKING_TIME = 1 (75 us), IDISS_TIME = 1 (75 us); SAMPLE_TIME is LRA-only and left at 3. CONTROL1 = 0x93, CONTROL2 = 0xF5.

Value Formula (datasheet) Result RATED_VOLTAGE Eq. 4: V = 21.18 mV x RV, so RV = floor(3000 / 21.18) 141 (0x8D) = 2.986 V OD_CLAMP Eq. 8: V = 21.64 mV x OD x (4.8 ms - 300 us) / (4.8 ms + 75 us + 75 us), so OD = floor(3600 / 19.673 mV) 182 (0xB6) = 3.580 V (183 would give 3.6001 V, over the limit) FEEDBACK (pre-cal) ERM, brake factor 2, loop gain 2, BEMF gain 2 (power-on default; calibration overwrites it) 0x2A CONTROL3 ERM_OPEN_LOOP cleared (power-on default is open loop), RTP format signed 0x80 CONTROL4 AUTO_CAL_TIME = 3 (1000-1200 ms) 0x30

Brake factor 2, loop gain 2 and AUTO_CAL_TIME 3 are the "valid for most actuators" values in the datasheet calibration procedure. The floors are deliberate: the register never exceeds the requested voltage. The output cannot exceed the DRV2605L supply either (3.3 V on the breakout unless VIN is higher), so the real ceiling on this bench is the supply, not 3.6 V.

docs.title: Real-time playback
docs.text: Signed format (the power-on default). Closed loop (bidirectional): 0x00 = no drive, 0x7F (127) = full rated voltage, 0x3F about half; negative values act as zero. Open loop: 0x7F = +OD_CLAMP, 0x81 = -OD_CLAMP (reverse drive). The ramp test uses 0 to 127 to 0, which is safe in both.

docs.title: Click latency
docs.text: hal_haptic_click_prepare(effect) loads the sequencer once; hal_haptic_click() is then a single two-byte I2C write (GO). Test 7 times that call with the microsecond clock. It measures the host-side I2C cost only; motor current and mechanical onset cannot be measured on this bench (no current sense or scope hook).

docs.title: Test menu (i2c_test)
docs.text:
Flash with scripts/flash.sh rp2350 i2c_test; menu on UART0 at 115200. q stops a running test (any key stops the effect sweep).

Key Test Notes 1 Bus scan idle-line check, scan 0x08-0x77, PASS when 0x36 and 0x5A answer; retries at 100 kHz if a device is missing or errors occur 2 Gauge dumps version/config, then 10 s of voltage, SOC and rate; SKIP if no battery 3 Gauge under load 5 s idle, 10 s with backlight 100 % and CPU busy; backlight is turned off at the end. Shows nothing if the Pico is USB-powered: the load current must flow from the battery through the gauge 4 Haptic ID STATUS, device ID (must be 7), mode, library, control registers 5 Haptic calibrate closed loop only (SKIP in open loop): auto-calibration (motor spins about 1 s); prints the measured values, then notes the restore, and a build-flag snippet 6 Haptic sweep effects 1-123, 300 ms apart (1-10 only in run-all) 7 Click latency 20 clicks, min/avg/max microseconds 8 Haptic RTP amplitude ramp 0 to 127 to 0 over 2 s 9 Soak 60 s: gauge read every 500 ms, click every 2 s; PASS only with zero I2C errors and recoveries ("clicks only" if the gauge is absent)

docs.text: Use Effect ID Wheel click 1 (Strong Click 100 %), provisional default; not yet chosen (test 6 sweep not run) Button click tbd Alert tbd

docs.title: When something fails
docs.text: Symptom Meaning Scan: nothing answers No ACK at all: check SDA GP20 / SCL GP21 wiring, breakout power, and that the breakout pull-ups are present Scan: lines low before start A device is holding the bus; the test tries recovery. If it stays low, power-cycle the breakouts 0x36 missing, 0x5A fine Gauge is powered from the battery side: connect a charged LiPo (a flat one makes 0x36 vanish) 0x5A missing DRV2605L power (3.3 V), wiring or EN pin Test 4: device ID not 7 A different chip or a bad read Test 5: calibration fails or never finishes Wrong ERM/LRA setting, or the motor is not connected/seated Test 9 reports errors Look at the stats line: NACKs or timeouts point at wiring or pull-ups; try 100 kHz

docs.title: Phase 1 — Pico 2 W prototype rig
docs.text:
Plan: a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W (or Pimoroni Pico Plus 2 W) on a breadboard/perfboard, wired to the donor's click wheel, LCD, headphone flex and battery via FPC breakout boards, to develop the drivers and UI before any custom PCB.

Item Why Source ~Cost Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W RP2350A, 4 MB flash, CYW43439 Wi-Fi/BT, 26 GPIO. The baseline. Pimoroni, The Pi Hut, Farnell, RS £6–7 Pimoroni Pico Plus 2 W RP2350B (48 GPIO), 16 MB flash, 8 MB PSRAM, same CYW43439 radio, USB-C. Closer to the final board — PSRAM for album art and audio buffers, more pins for a 16-bit LCD bus. Preferred dev board. Pimoroni ~£17 Pico Debug Probe SWD debugging + UART; essential once drivers get involved Pimoroni, Pi Hut ~£12 FPC/FFC breakout boards, 0.5 mm pitch, 50-pin (for the ER-TFT024IPS-3) Brings the panel out to 2.54 mm headers eBay / AliExpress ("FPC 0.5mm 50 pin adapter board") £2–4 FPC breakout boards for the iPod click wheel, LCD and headphone flexes Pitch/pin count to be measured on the donor; buy a 0.3/0.4/0.5 mm assortment eBay / AliExpress £5 for a mixed pack Second donor Classic or a spare click wheel + headphone flex Spares for the inevitable torn ribbon eBay UK, Elite Obsolete £10–30 I²S DAC breakout (PCM5102A) Stand-in for the CS43131 until the custom board; proves the audio pipeline Pimoroni (Pico Audio Pack), Pi Hut, eBay £4–15 microSD breakout (SPI/SDIO) Storage during prototyping Adafruit via Pi Hut, eBay £3–5 1,000–2,000 mAh LiPo with JST-PH + LiPo SHIM / charger board Battery power on the bench Pimoroni (LiPo SHIM for Pico), Pi Hut £8–15 Logic analyser (Saleae-compatible 8ch or DSLogic) Sniffing the stock board's click-wheel serial line and LCD bus before it's retired eBay, Pi Hut £10–60

Tip: before removing the original logic board, probe the wheel and LCD ribbons live to confirm Rockbox's pinouts against this exact board revision.
