docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Exported from the neuPod design doc (Requirements tab, 25 Oct – 1 Nov 2026). Prices are approximate UK low-volume figures. The supplier and parts list is on the Reference page; the engineering detail is on the Design page.

docs.title: Goal and scope
docs.text:
Design a drop-in replacement logic board for the iPod Classic 6G/7G that adds Wi-Fi, Bluetooth audio, microSD storage and USB-C, while reusing the original shell, click wheel and (optionally) screen.

  • Fully reversible: original board, drive and battery can go back in.
  • No soldering to original iPod parts; board connects to the existing flex cables.
  • Fills a gap: no existing product gives a Classic Wi-Fi (Sprout targets 3G/4G/mini only; Moonlit, Boxy Pixel and iFlash add BT/USB-C/storage but keep the stock SoC).
  • Target sizes: thin shell first (the donor in hand), thick shell as the easier variant.

docs.title: Target hardware
docs.text:
Donor in hand: Apple iPod Classic 6th generation, model A1238, EMC 2173, 120 GB — the thin shell (bought on eBay, 25 Oct 2026).

Item Thin Classic (120 GB, late 160 GB) Thick Classic (80 GB, early 160 GB) Overall thickness ~10.5 mm ~13.5 mm Internal depth (approx) ~8 mm ~11 mm Stock battery ~550–650 mAh ~850 mAh Stock HDD 5 mm, 1.8" ZIF 8 mm, 1.8" ZIF Opening Spring clips, stiffer Spring clips

Why 6G/7G over 4G/5G: cheapest donors (£20–40 dead-HDD units), 320×240 colour panel, bigger wheel, and the LCD/wheel were reverse-engineered by Rockbox. 6G vs 7G makes no difference to a replacement board (same shell, screen, wheel). A thin-to-thick rear-shell swap (~£10) is a cheap way to gain battery depth.

Opening: iFixit guide iPod Classic Logic Board Replacement #572. Thin metal opening tools; release clips along both long edges; open like a book hinged at the bottom-left; disconnect battery flex (bottom) and headphone/hold flex (top, ZIF) before separating; HDD on a ZIF ribbon — flip the latch before pulling.

docs.title: Compute options
docs.text:
Current preference: RP2350B as the always-on brain (Sprout Pico approach), with a footprint reserved for a Linux module (Raspberry Pi Compute Module Zero or ESP32-P4) if streaming apps are wanted later.

Raspberry Pi's Broadcom application processors (BCM2710/2711/2712, the Zero 2 W's RP3A0 SiP) are not sold to third parties, so only their microcontrollers (RP2040/RP2350) can go on a custom PCB.

Option Cores / clock RAM Wi-Fi/BT Linux PCB layers Unit cost Notes RP2350B 2× Cortex-M33 (or RISC-V) @ 150 MHz 520 KB SRAM + QSPI PSRAM (up to 8 MB) External No 4 ~£1 48 GPIO; RP2354 variants have 2 MB flash in-package; instant-on; ~40 h battery class; PIO+DMA drives parallel LCD RP2040 2× Cortex-M0+ @ 133 MHz 264 KB External No 4 ~£0.70 Too little RAM/CPU for colour UI + codecs; avoid ESP32-S3 2× Xtensa LX7 @ 240 MHz 512 KB + 8 MB PSRAM On-chip (2.4 GHz n, BLE 5) No 4 ~£2–3 Simplest single-chip Wi-Fi/BT route; classic BT A2DP needs the older ESP32, S3 is BLE-only (LE Audio) Allwinner T113-S3 2× Cortex-A7 @ 1.2 GHz 128 MB DDR3 in-package External module Mainline 4 ~£4–5 QFN128, hand-reworkable; best fully-custom Linux route Rockchip RV1106 Cortex-A7 @ 1.2 GHz 256 MB in-package External Yes 4 ~£4–6 Luckfox Pico reference design Zero 2 W as module 4× Cortex-A53 @ 1 GHz (RP3A0) 512 MB LPDDR2 CYW43438 on-board Yes Carrier only ~£14 65×30×~1 mm; 6-layer board; soldered to a custom carrier; 0.3–0.6 W idle Compute Module Zero as Zero 2 W 512 MB On module Yes Carrier only ~£15–20 What Sprout Pi uses; check availability

Avoid any SoC needing external DDR (6–8 layers, impedance control).

docs.title: Connectivity
docs.text:
Required: 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, Bluetooth audio (A2DP to AirPods/headphones/speakers), USB-C for charging and drag-and-drop file transfer (mass storage), digital audio out over USB-C.

  • Radio for RP2350 route: Infineon CYW43439 over SPI (Pico W / Pico 2 W reference design is open, ~£2–3 + antenna) or an ESP32-C6 as radio co-processor over SPI (~£1.50, Wi-Fi 6 + BLE 5 only, easier to source). The C6 has no classic Bluetooth, so no A2DP; it only suits Wi-Fi.
  • Classic Bluetooth A2DP is needed for most headphones; confirm the chosen radio supports BR/EDR, not just BLE.
  • Antenna (requirement, 3 Nov 2026): the shell is a Faraday cage; the only RF-transparent area is the top plastic window of the 6G back. The antenna sits there with its keep-out, and the radio module chosen must have a u.FL connector or an on-module antenna that can be placed there. Applies to Bluetooth first.
  • Final-board radio: not a bare CYW43439 (not assemblable at JLCPCB, outside the BTstack grant). Options: RM2 module, or an ESP32 with its own stack — see ADR-0007.
  • USB-C: 5.1 kΩ CC pulldowns for 5 V from C-to-C cables; USB 2.0 data; no PD needed at 1–2 A. The 30-pin aperture (~21 × 3 mm) takes a mid-mount USB-C receptacle with a small printed/CNC filler.
  • GPIO: 2× spare via the wired-remote connector (as Sprout) is a nice-to-have.

Existing kits for reference: Moonlit Market Classic Connect 2 (BT 5.2 aptX, Qi, haptics, USB-C charge; sync needs soldering), Boxy Pixel (BT 5.0 + USB-C charge only).

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
microSD, SDXC up to 2 TB, via SDIO (4-bit) for throughput; exFAT so the card is readable on a PC.

  • Push-push or hinged socket, accessible without opening the case is not possible on a Classic, so a reliable internal socket is enough.
  • Keep a 2 TB card on the test list: controller compatibility is where iFlash users hit trouble.
  • Library index/metadata cached in PSRAM or on-card database to keep browse fast with 100k+ tracks.
  • Card power (requirement, 3 Nov 2026): GPIO-controlled load switch on card VDD, so a wedged card can be power-cycled. SD clock from integer dividers only; multi-block reads capped at 128 blocks (Storage).

docs.title: Display
docs.text:
Preferred upgrade: a 2.4"–2.8" IPS TFT (ST7789V / ILI9341, 240×320) replacing the stock panel; keep the stock panel as plan B.

Option Size / resolution Interface Cost Pros Cons Stock 6G/7G panel 2.5", 320×240 TN 8080-style parallel (init sequence in Rockbox ipod6g) £0 (reused) No mechanical change; fully reversible Dim, low contrast; must be driven exactly as Rockbox does IPS TFT, ST7789V / ILI9341 2.4" (~60 × 42 mm active) to 2.8", 240×320 SPI or 8080 parallel; RP2350 PIO+DMA £3–6 bare panel Near-OLED contrast; trivial to drive; what Zac Builds used Needs masking/bezel fit to the Classic window; new FPC routing Mono OLED (SSD1309 / SSD1322) 2.4–2.7", 128×64 or 256×64 SPI / 8080 £5–15 Retro Sprout look; very low power No album art, no colour Colour OLED ≤1.5" at 128×128; larger are MIPI phone panels SPI, or MIPI needing a bridge varies — Nothing practical at 2.5" 320×240; rule out

Requirement: measure the Classic's window aperture and the LCD bay in the mid-frame before choosing a panel part number.

Shortlisted panel: EastRising ER-TFT024IPS-3 — 2.4" IPS 240×320, ST7789V, bare glass, 50-pin 0.5 mm FPC. Active 36.72 × 48.96 mm, visual 38.72 × 50.96 mm, outline 42.72 × 59.26 × 2.3 mm (stock Classic panel ≈ 38 × 51 mm active, so ~1 mm margin each edge). 8080 8/9/16/18-bit, SPI, RGB; 500:1, 300 cd/m², 80° all round; VDD 2.8 V typ, backlight 4 WLED 70 mA. $6.35 direct; module version ER-TFTM024IPS-3 on eBay (BuyDisplay) ~$12.60 for prototyping. Datasheet, STEP model, ST7789V datasheet and ZIF drawing on the product page. Alternative: Ronbo RB024D12N19B (same glass, 12-pin SPI-only FPC).

Premium option: 2.4" AMOLED 450×600, Raydium RM690B0 (DisplayModule DM-AMOLED240-011, also Anders, TailorPixels, SWICN; ~£45–50 single, ~$25 Alibaba lots). Same 36.72 × 48.96 mm active area as the IPS panel so it fits the window identically; 311 ppi, 24-bit, 100,000:1, 60 Hz; QSPI/SPI/MIPI. Needs an AMOLED PMIC (TPS65632-class, AVDD ~4.6 V / ELVSS negative) and a QSPI write path (PIO on RP2350 at reduced frame rate, native on ESP32-S3). Burn-in and content-dependent power are the trade-offs. Ruled out: no OLED exists in the Classic's native 2.5" 4:3 landscape; memory-in-pixel, e-paper, micro-LED and phone MIPI AMOLEDs don't suit. Final board could carry both the 50-pin IPS and the AMOLED FPC footprints.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
Hi-fi DAC with headphone amp driving the original 3.5 mm jack via the existing headphone/hold-switch flex, plus Bluetooth A2DP and USB-C digital audio out.

  • Codec (3 Nov 2026, ADR-0012, proposed): ES8311 baseline, ES8388 alternative, PCM5102A as the DAC-only no-MCLK fallback. CS43131 dropped (≈42 pcs at LCSC). Open point: the ES8311 is mono.
  • I²S from the MCU; the board provides MCLK (256 fs from clk_gpout), but the codec must also run with its PLL from BCLK.
  • Audio isolation (requirement): audio runs on a dedicated bare-metal core with lock-free rings only (ADR-0011); any SoC candidate needs a spare core.
  • Codecs required: MP3, AAC, ALAC, FLAC, Opus (software decode on RP2350 is fine at 150 MHz).
  • Optional: small LRA for haptic click-wheel feedback (~£1, as Moonlit's kit).

Single jack, line or headphone: one 3.5 mm output from the DAC's headphone driver serves both; the codec's load/jack detection (CS43131 had this; check the ADR-0012 part) can switch a firmware "line mode" (fixed level, volume bypassed) when a high-impedance load is seen. No separate line-out socket.

Optional: optical S/PDIF via a mini-TOSLINK combo jack (Apple-style). Parts: 3.5 mm optical-combo socket with integrated IR transmitter (Everlight PLT133/T10W-series, Cliff FCR684206 or similar, ~£2–4; check barrel depth against the Classic's jack aperture). Signal generated by an RP2350 PIO state machine (biphase-mark, 64× fs) from the same audio buffer as I²S; route to S/PDIF and bypass volume when an optical plug is detected. The jack then lives on the new board rather than on the original headphone flex (flex still used for the hold switch).

Audio quality policy: lossless end-to-end on every wired/digital path. Decode once to a 32-bit mixer; no resampling unless the sink requires it; bit-perfect FLAC/ALAC to the DAC (CS43131: 32/384, ~130 dB DNR), to optical S/PDIF (24/96) and to USB-C UAC2. Dedicated low-noise analogue LDO and a 22.5792/24.576 MHz clock pair (or DAC PLL) for the DAC. Decode target: 24/96 FLAC on RP2350 (24/192 only on ESP32-S3-class).

Bluetooth codec Max bitrate Available on CYW43439 + BTstack Available on an external QCC module SBC / SBC-XQ 328k / ~500k Yes Yes AAC 256k 256k Encoder not free (FDK licence, heavy on M33) Yes aptX / aptX HD 352k / 576k No (Qualcomm licence) Yes LDAC 990k No (Sony licence) Some modules LC3 (LE Audio) ~345k Immature Varies

Decision pending: Bluetooth path = SBC-XQ on the CYW43439 (simplest, no extra parts) or an external Qualcomm QCC3008/3040/5125 transmitter module on I²S with UART control (aptX HD/AAC/LDAC, what the commercial iPod BT kits use). Wi-Fi/BT coexistence and the metal shell limit link quality either way.

Recording (new requirement, 31 Oct 2026): the board shall record audio to microSD. Sources, in priority order: (1) mono mic on a 4-pole headset plugged into the 3.5 mm jack; (2) Bluetooth headset mic (HFP, voice quality only); (3) optional on-board MEMS mic for voice notes; (4) USB-C audio in. Target formats: WAV 48 kHz/16-bit for the jack and MEMS paths; whatever the BT profile delivers for HFP. The codec/DAC chosen must therefore include an ADC input (CS43131 is DAC-only — either add a small ADC such as a PCM1808/ES8311/WM8960-class codec, or move to a combined codec part). Keep the ADC analogue front end on its own clean LDO, away from the switcher, same as the DAC.

3.5 mm jack = 4-pole TRRS, CTIA pinout (tip L, ring 1 R, ring 2 GND, sleeve mic). Requirements:

  • Mic bias ~2.0–2.7 V via ~2.2 kΩ, switchable off in firmware.
  • Inline-button decode: headsets short the mic line through resistors (play/pause ≈ 0 Ω, vol+ ≈ 240 Ω, vol− ≈ 600 Ω); read with an ADC channel on the mic line and map to click-wheel actions.
  • Jack insert detect (switched contact on the socket or codec jack-detect) to route headphone/line/optical and to disable mic bias when a 3-pole TRS plug is present (its sleeve is ground).
  • Design for CTIA only; OMTP (mic/GND swapped) headsets are not supported.
  • The optical-combo socket option above must still be 4-pole if chosen; check availability (optical + TRRS combos are rarer than optical + TRS).

Bluetooth profiles required: A2DP source for stereo playback — neuPod sends audio to the headphones/speaker, which are the A2DP sink (SBC/AAC minimum; aptX/LDAC per the transmitter decision above). AVRCP (neuPod as target, the headset as controller) for play/pause/next/previous from the headset buttons, plus absolute volume so the headset's volume and neuPod's are one control. HFP in the Audio Gateway role for the headset mic — note it drops both directions to 8/16 kHz mono (CVSD/mSBC), so BT recording is voice-note quality only. LE Audio / LC3 (stereo, bidirectional, good quality) is a nice-to-have: pick a radio whose stack can do LE Audio so it can be enabled later. Reference headset for testing: Stuart's AirPods Pro 3 (model A3063/A3064, 2025, Apple H2) — A2DP + AAC for playback, HFP for mic; LE Audio only via Apple's own path, so not usable for LC3 testing.

docs.title: Power and battery
docs.text:
Target: 2,000+ mAh in the thin shell, 3,000 mAh in the thick shell; 40 h Bluetooth playback is the benchmark (Sprout's figure with 2,500 mAh).

Shell Cell thickness available Candidate cells Capacity Thin (donor) ~4 mm once HDD + original board are gone (~1 mm board) 405080, 4055100-class pouch ~2,000–2,500 mAh Thick ~6–7 mm 605070 / 605080, 7 mm variants ~3,000–3,500 mAh Stock reference thin 550–650 mAh, thick 850 mAh; aftermarket thin ~1,000–1,200 mAh, thick 3,000 mAh (with stock board + iFlash)
  • Cells with built-in PCM (OV/UV/OC protection); thermistor input on the board.
  • Charger (3 Nov 2026): BQ25895 (I²C 0x6A, INT pin, full status registers, OTG, power-path). Firmware models its state machine in hal_charger.h; the testbed (Micro-Lipo MCP73831, no STAT pin) is a second implementation: VBUS present (cyw43 WL_GPIO2) AND MAX17048 CRATE > 0 = charging; VBUS AND CRATE ≈ 0 AND SOC ≥ 98 % = full.
  • Fuel gauge for real percentage in the UI: BQ27441 or MAX17048.
  • Rails: 3.3 V for MCU/radio/SD, clean analogue rail for the DAC, LCD backlight boost.
  • Power states: instant-on from sleep (RP2350 dormant mode), deep sleep when hold is on, hard off.

Power budget by state (estimates, to be measured on the bench):

Block Standby Playing, screen off, BT RP2350 core ~1 mA sleep / 0.2 mA dormant 25–40 mA ESP32-S3 core + octal PSRAM ~10 µA deep sleep / ~2 mA light 60–100 mA CYW43439 BT A2DP <1 mA 30–50 mA QCC3008-class BT module ~1 mA 20–35 mA microSD <0.2 mA ~10 mA average (bursts to 60) CS43131 DAC + HP amp off 10–25 mA 2.4" IPS + backlight off 100–150 mA when on 2.4" AMOLED off 40–200 mA when on, content dependent Regulators, gauge, misc ~1 mA ~5 mA

Totals playing to BT, screen off: architecture A (RP2350 + CYW43439) ~80–110 mA → 23–30 h on 2,500 mAh; architecture B (ESP32-S3 + QCC) ~110–160 mA → 16–22 h. Standby target <0.5 mA: load switches on SD, DAC and radio rails; wake from hold switch or wheel. Backlight dims to ~10% after the idle time (default 30 s) and goes fully off 3 min after that (Settings > Display, both adjustable; ADR-0020; this replaces the earlier "off within ~15 s": the totals above assume the screen off, so a listening session pays the 3.5 minutes of display once, after each press); Wi-Fi off during playback; core clock scaled to the minimum that keeps the audio buffer full.

docs.title: Reused parts and mechanical
docs.text:
Reuse the shell, mid-frame, click wheel and its FPC, headphone/hold-switch flex, and (plan B) the LCD. Everything connects via the original ribbons into FPC/ZIF connectors on the new board.

Known internal geometry (open sources; everything else comes from the donor scan): envelope 103.5 × 61.8 × 10.5 mm thin / 13.5 mm thick (everymac). Stack front→back: front plate + glass; click wheel and LCD on a steel backing plate; metal mid-frame; logic board (full footprint, ~95 × 55 × 1.0 mm, two screws to the frame, connectors on its edges and back face); battery pouch on the board; 1.8" ZIF HDD in foam bumpers — Toshiba MK8022GAA/MK1231GAL/MK1634GAL, 54 × 71 × 5 mm thin or 8 mm thick; stainless back shell (iFixit teardown). Usable depth for our board + cell: ~6 mm thin, ~9 mm thick. Board silicon and revisions (A1238 120 GB = Rev A, 2008): S5L8702, K4X51163PE SDRAM, SST25VF080B flash, PCF50635 PMU, CS42L55 codec, LTC4066 charger (freemyipod). Not published anywhere: board/mid-frame drawings, 6G connector pitches, battery outline, screw positions.

  • Board outline: match the original logic board's outline and the mid-frame screw holes (two Phillips screws); design to the mid-frame, not the shell. Original board ~1.6 mm; target 1.0–1.2 mm.
  • Connectors to provide: click wheel FPC, LCD FPC (stock pinout or new panel), headphone/hold flex, battery (3-pin, thermistor), microSD socket, USB-C mid-mount.
  • Click wheel: keep; serial protocol documented in Rockbox; new wheels available from Elite Obsolete.
  • Port aperture: 30-pin opening ~21 × 3 mm; USB-C with printed/CNC filler. Keep the port centred.
  • Antenna keep-out: near the headphone jack's plastic insert or under the wheel.
  • Thermal/EMI: metal shell; no thermal issue at RP2350 power levels.
  • Reversibility: no adhesive on original parts; foam spacers where the HDD was.
  • Cosmetic parts if needed: Elite Obsolete (shells, wheels, faceplates), Moonlit Market, iFlash (shells, screws, tools).

Click wheel sub-board (how it works): a capacitive ring of ~16 copper segments under the plastic plus five dome switches, scanned by a microcontroller on the flex itself (Cypress PSoC on the 5G; same family on the 6G). The PSoC interpolates finger position to 96 steps per revolution and streams 32-bit frames on its own ~53 kHz clock while touched; the host only listens (one init packet). It has its own 3.0 V LDO fed from the system rail. All the touch logic therefore stays in the wheel — our board needs 4 lines + power and a frame decoder (design doc §4.1).

Click feedback — direction set 3 Nov 2026: the final board carries both a piezo footprint (stock feel) and an LRA footprint (LD0832AA, stocked); A/B on the testbed before freezing. The Click feedback setting becomes piezo / haptic / off. Background: The stock iPod has no haptic: the click is a piezo buzzer on the logic board driven as a tone (Rockbox piezo-6g.c). Options: (a) piezo only — authentic, ~£0.50, one GPIO/PWM; (b) LRA or ERM haptic via DRV2605L on I²C — the Moonlit Classic Connect feel, ~£5, needs board area near the wheel; (c) both, selectable in settings. Board footprints for both are cheap; the decision is about mid-frame space and whether the original feel matters.

docs.title: Firmware
docs.text:
Click-wheel-driven UI recreating the Classic experience (menus, Cover Flow, podcasts, search), audio pipeline with software codecs, BT/Wi-Fi stacks, USB mass storage. This is the largest cost in the project — more than the hardware.

  • Starting points: Rockbox ipod6g target (LCD init, click wheel protocol, headphone detect); Sprout's open-source firmware (MPL-2.0) once published at github.com/seanpod/sprout; sPot (Guy Dupont) for a Pi/Spotify UI.
  • Wi-Fi use cases: podcast download, library sync from a NAS/PC, firmware OTA. Streaming (Spotify/Apple Music) needs a Linux module.
  • Host side: the iPod must mount as a plain USB drive — no iTunes dependency.
  • Keep the stock-panel driver and a new-panel driver behind one display abstraction so either screen works.
  • RAM budget: every feature ADR states its RAM cost (the Pico 2 W's 520 KB is no longer a limit since 12 Nov 2026: the product target is the RP2350B with PSRAM, ADR-0001 amendment). The final board has 8 MB PSRAM (APS6404L, QSPI CS1, ADR-0013); artwork, HTTP and AAC are PSRAM-only.
  • Flash and OTA: final board 16 MB W25Q128; bootrom A/B partitions with TBYB (ADR-0014).
  • Secrets: RP2350 random 256-bit key in OTP at provisioning, chip-ID HKDF as the pre-provisioning fallback, no secure element; ESP32 route: eFuse key + flash encryption. Secure boot decided later (Wi-Fi).
  • Clock: ADR-0015.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
About £35–55 in parts per board (RP2350 route ~£25–40), before the donor iPod and battery; budget £300–600 for two or three prototype spins including assembly. Figures are approximate, low-volume UK pricing, October 2026.

Item Estimate Compute: RP2350B / ESP32-S3 / T113 £1–5 Compute: Zero 2 W or CM Zero (module route) £14–20 DAC + headphone amp (CS43131 / ES9018K2M) £5–8 Charger, fuel gauge, regulators £4–6 Wi-Fi/BT (CYW43439 or ESP32-C6, if not on-chip) £2–5 microSD socket, USB-C, FPC/ZIF connectors £3–4 Passives, crystals, ESD, antenna £3–5 PCB, 4-layer, JLCPCB, 5 pcs £20–40 per batch (6-layer ~double) Assembly £5–15 per board, or hand-build Battery 2,000–3,000 mAh £10–15 Donor Classic £25–40 (already bought) Replacement IPS panel (optional) £3–6 Thick rear shell (optional) ~£10

docs.title: Runtime: RTOS, audio core and boot
docs.text: The neupod executable (RP2350 and host) is this runtime. Decisions: ADR-0011 (single-core FreeRTOS on core 0, bare-metal audio core on core 1; amends ADR-0009) and ADR-0010 (LVGL). The RTOS task table lives in app/include/runtime_config.h; this page explains it.

docs.title: Cores
docs.text: Core Runs Rules 0 FreeRTOS (single-core kernel): UI, input, storage, monitor, CYW43 worker, boot checks normal RTOS code 1 the bare-metal audio core: a main loop (commands + "decoder": silence, test signals, WAV conversion) and the sink's block interrupt (the I2S DMA interrupt); no kernel the core-1 rules below

docs.title: Core-1 rules
docs.text: Core 1 code (app/audio/audio_core.c, audio_shared.c, audio_dsp.c, spsc_ring.c, the headers they use, and platforms/rp2350/hal/hal_audio.c / hal_audio_null.c) must not use: FreeRTOS or os.h; stdio (printf); malloc; any SDK primitive the FreeRTOS interop reroutes to the kernel (mutex, semaphore, queue, critical section, sleep_*, busy_wait_*); hal_delay_ms. It talks to core 0 only through lock-free rings and a seqlock. Hardware registers, the 1 MHz timer reads (time_us_64, hal_micros) and the SDK's spin-lock-only alarm API are fine. The ctest audio_core_rules (cmake/check_core1_rules.cmake) fails the build on forbidden tokens in those files.

docs.title: Hot path in RAM
docs.text: on_block, the ring functions, the alarm interrupt (block_isr, driven straight from the timer registers, no SDK alarm code and no spin lock shared with core 0) and hal_micros run from RAM (NEUPOD_RAM_FUNC, __not_in_flash_func) so the audio core does not contend with the UI for the XIP flash cache. memcpy and memset (newlib, flash) are still used by the ring. Core 1's stack is painted at start and its high-water mark is printed in the audio line (core1_stack_free=).

docs.title: Core 0 / core 1 communication
docs.text:
From to Mechanism core 0 to 1: commands ring of audio_cmd_t (open, close, statistics window, volume, tone, stream start, stream next, pause, stop); several core-0 tasks send, so audio_ctl.c serialises them with a mutex core 0 to 1: stream data byte ring, 32 KB, fed by the storage task while a file plays: raw WAV bytes, compressed FLAC / MP3 bytes, or length-prefixed ALAC packets core 0 to 1: stream slots two slots (seq & 1) with the stream description and its byte length (published once its last byte is in the ring), plus g_audio_next_valid (the announced successor, cleared to cancel); see Audio core 1 to 0: seek request request counter plus byte offset, acknowledged by core 0, flush acknowledged by core 1 (stream_io.h) core 1 to 0: handshake counters written only by core 1: streams set up / ended with nothing following (core 0 must not write data for a new stream before the first moves), the sequence number of the open decoder, and gapless handoffs completed (written by the block interrupt) core 1 to 0: events two rings (one per producer: the block interrupt, the main loop): stream opened/closed, underrun (at most ~1/s), end of track, command error core 1 to 0: statistics seqlock-published audio_stats_t, written only by the block interrupt inside core 1: decoder to sink PCM ring, 4096 stereo int32 frames (16 blocks, 93 ms at 44.1 kHz)

Every ring has exactly one producer and one consumer (spsc_ring.h: acquire/release loads and stores only, no read-modify-write, so it is safe across the two cores).

docs.title: How audio timing works
docs.text: With NEUPOD_AUDIO_SINK=null (or on the host) the sink arms a 1 MHz hardware alarm from core 1; its interrupt fires every 256 frames (5.8 ms at 44.1 kHz) on absolute deadlines (no drift) and runs on_block, which reads one block from the PCM ring (silence and an underrun if the decoder starved it), applies the volume ramp, hands it to the sink and updates the statistics and the amp mute line. The interrupt preempts the decoder (-DNEUPOD_DECODER_LOAD_PCT=25 makes it busy-spend 25 % of a block period per block, as the old stub did, to prove it), so block timing does not depend on decoder time. The main loop sleeps with WFI when idle. Nothing on core 0 can delay it: no shared lock, no kernel, no shared interrupt. The I2S sink (default on the RP2350, see Audio) uses the same structure with the DMA block-complete interrupt (DMA_IRQ_1, core 1) instead of the alarm.

docs.title: RTOS tasks (core 0)
docs.text:
Priority 7 is the highest; the kernel idle task is 0.

Task Priority Stack Period / trigger Budget kernel timer service 6 1.5 KB kernel timers microseconds storage 5 8 KB request queue; while a file streams, every 1 ms; otherwise every 500 ms directory listings and volume space for the UI (yields every 32 entries); streams the file from the card in 2 KB reads into the audio data ring; decodes the album art of the playing track in slices (2 ms of work, 1 ms sleep, audio top-ups between, aborts on any request; UI); loads the settings store after the card mounts and saves it about 1.5 s after a change (Bluetooth); later: library scan, track prefetch input 4 2 KB every 2 ms well under 1 % (the wheel FIFO overflows after ~4.8 ms); also the Power key and Hold switch levels I2C users, while on the bus 4 (lifted) n/a boot checks, the 5 s gauge read a few ms (see findings) CYW43 worker (SDK) 3 6 KB radio events; every BTstack callback and lwIP callback LED; Bluetooth (BTstack's one thread); lwIP (via the SDK's FreeRTOS arch; lwIP also has its own 4 KB tcpip thread) wifi (policy) 1 4 KB every 200 ms requests from the UI, join/retry with backoff, power policy, SNTP, the 1 s snapshot for the UI (Wi-Fi) haptic (click feedback) 4 2 KB click queue (2 deep, non-blocking for the UI) a few ms per click; back to standby after 2 s idle UI (LVGL) 2 12 KB 5 to 30 ms, from LVGL's own timer frame strip render + 24-line blocking DMA monitor 1 3 KB 100 ms tick: heartbeat 1 s, gauge 5 s, stats 10 s negligible boot checks (transient, 6) 1 3 to 5 KB once at boot bounded by per-check deadlines

Core 1 has its own 16 KB stack array and a 116 KB codec arena (both static RAM). Heap: heap_4, 80 KB (NEUPOD_RTOS_HEAP_BYTES, app/os/memory_budget.h), holds task stacks and kernel objects; static RAM beyond that is the LVGL pool (72 KB, NEUPOD_LVGL_POOL_BYTES), the BTstack pools (about 7 KB), the settings store (about 5 KB), the two render buffers (30 KB), the album-art thumbnail (8 KB, app/runtime/art_service.c), the directory-listing buffer (about 19 KB) and the audio core's rings and block buffer (about 28 KB), the play queue (about 3.9 KB, plus a 264 B rollback snapshot) and two track contexts for the stream controller (2.8 KB). The monitor prints the heap low-water mark and each task's lowest free stack every 10 s. Input is above the UI so wheel frames are never lost while LVGL renders; the monitor is lowest; boot-check tasks sit below the UI so the splash keeps animating while they run.

docs.title: Inter-task data (core 0)
docs.text: From to Mechanism input to UI queue of input_event_t (RT_INPUT_QUEUE_LEN = 64 deep). Wheel and key events are dropped if the UI lags, and counted (input: WARNING n events dropped in the 10 s statistics when it ever happens); Power-key and Hold-switch edges are retried until the queue takes them. UI-6: the queue was 16 deep (8 presses, two events each) and the UI drained it once per pass (a frame, about 30 ms, then its sleep), so a burst of more than 8 presses (a UART paste, a quick run on the keypad) lost the rest silently and later keys landed on the wrong screen; the UI now sleeps on the queue (an arriving event wakes it at once) and the queue holds 32 presses monitor / battery check to UI latest value in a mutex-guarded store (battery_store) boot checks to UI capabilities_t (mutex-guarded; first result per subsystem wins) I2C bus one mutex (rt_i2c_mutex) around every battery / haptic transaction UI to haptic task 2-deep byte queue, sent without waiting (rt_haptic_click) UI to player player.h: a mutex-guarded state (what plays, volume) plus commands to the audio core; the storage task reports file start and errors; end of file and stream faults are read back from the audio core's counters and statistics radio worker to UI hal_bt_event_fn callback turned into a 16-deep queue of hal_bt_event_t by bt_service.c (state, device found/named, scan done); non-blocking send, dropped if the UI lags. Link events (pairing, connection state) are not queued: the callback hands them to bt_saved_on_event (RAM-only settings write) and screens read hal_bt_link_state() anyone to settings store settings_store.h: RAM image behind a mutex; only the storage task reads or writes the card file UI to storage task request queue (list a directory, free space, settings load, and the music library: open an index, fill a window of rows, build the index); results come back on a result queue and the UI polls it, the library's answers in a small mailbox it polls the same way. The entries live in one static buffer that the UI reads only after the result for its latest request arrived; the library's reader and row window share that same buffer (the Files screen and the Music screens are never on screen together), so the library adds no RAM for them. Why a task: an SD directory scan is hundreds of sector reads and the UI task must never stall, and FatFs is not re-entrant

docs.title: UI performance
docs.text: The monitor prints every 10 s ui: frames=… frame_us avg/max=… lvgl_mem=used/total (max …, frag …%): passes of lv_timer_handler that rendered something (render plus the blocking strip flush), their average and worst time in the window, and LVGL pool use. Each list screen costs about 15 KB of the pool (its rows are a fixed pool of objects, whatever the item count), so the pool is 72 KB (it was 96 KB until the BTstack stack needed the room; the bench peak was about 38 KB) and the stack is limited to 8 screens. The host tour also prints ui: screen '<name>' lvgl_mem=… at every snapshot.

docs.title: What the monitor prints about audio
docs.text:
Every 10 s:

audio sink: i2s rate=44099.488 Hz (requested 44100 Hz, clkdiv=22+37/256) dma_underruns=0 muted=1 source=none audible=0 volume=-30dB pcm_frames=0
audio: blocks=1861 underruns=0 sink_missed=0 period_us min/avg/max=5431/5804/6181 (nominal 5804) jitter_max_us=377 ring_min=1792/4096 decoded=1868 data_bytes=0 events_dropped=0
cpu%(of one core)/stack-free-min: ... (core 0 tasks only)

blocks rises by about 1723 per 10 s (172 per second); the period and jitter figures are for the last 10 s window. Events (audio event: stream opened (44100), UNDERRUN) are printed as they arrive. A log-only stall check prints AUDIO CORE STALLED if the block counter stops for a second; it is silent on a good run. The figures above are from the host, where the clock is a timer thread on a PC; the RP2350 numbers are measured on the board. audio: stats unavailable / monitor: audio stats unavailable means the seqlock read gave up (core 1 stopped mid-update); the reader is bounded so the monitor keeps running.

docs.title: Bench findings (history)
docs.text:
These led to ADR-0011; the details are kept because they are the reason for the architecture.

  1. Event-list corruption. In the first design (SMP FreeRTOS, audio task woken by xSemaphoreGiveFromISR from an alarm interrupt on core 1) the board hung within a second: core 1 spun in vListInsert holding the kernel task lock, core 0 spun on it in PendSV, and the semaphore's wait list showed the audio task's event-list item inserted twice.
  2. Lost cross-core yield requests. With a polled audio wait, core 1 froze about 1.5 s in, in prvCheckForRunStateChange, waiting for a yield doorbell that never arrived. A watchdog that re-sent the doorbell recovered it every time ("AUDIO STALLED ... kicking core 1", "RECOVERED after 1 kick"), which proves the doorbell requests were being lost; with that workaround audio ran with 2 s outliers and 89 % decoder load. The kernel is the Raspberry Pi fork's SMP RP2350 port (its newest commit); upstream FreeRTOS-Kernel has no RP2350 port and its core cannot be combined with the fork's port.
  3. I2C timeouts in the haptic check. hal_i2c timeouts are wall-clock with a 2 ms floor and a transaction takes about 0.5 ms; a check task at priority 1 is pre-empted by the UI (priority 2) for a whole frame, so the transaction "timed out" on a healthy bus. The I2C users now run at priority 4 (RT_PRIO_I2C) while on the bus; the haptic check still leaves the DRV2605L in standby.
  4. CPU percentages. FreeRTOS attributes run time only when a task is switched out, so a task that runs uninterrupted is under-reported until it next switches; with the single-core kernel the idle figure is now meaningful. The percentages are shares of core 0. UI load of 10 to 20 % during the first 10 s is the splash (eight pulsing icons and the shimmer re-render two 24-line strips per frame with a blocking DMA wait); it falls once the static home screen is up.

docs.title: Boot sequence
docs.text:
1. main(): hal_system_init() (clocks, UART; unchanged order), then neupod_runtime_run() launches the audio core (core 1), opens the stream, creates the RTOS tasks and starts the scheduler.
  2. The UI task initialises the display first, draws the splash (wordmark, firmware version and git hash, one icon per subsystem) and only then switches the backlight on.
  3. It starts the boot checks, each in its own task with a deadline. All checks are read-only.
  4. Each icon pulses while its check runs, becomes solid when it passes, and gets a red cross only if the subsystem is not fully correct. The reason for each failure is printed on the UART (boot: storage DEGRADED: card init: NO_CARD).
  5. The splash holds until every check is resolved, at least 1.5 s (RT_SPLASH_MIN_MS) and at most 5 s for the checks themselves. If every check passed it fades to the home screen at once. If any icon has a cross, the splash is held for another 8 s (RT_SPLASH_HOLD_MS) from the moment the checks are done, with a thin bar along the bottom draining over the hold, and one failure reason at a time under the icons ([2/5] storage: card init: NO_CARD, 1.6 s each; all of them do not fit at 320x240). Any input event skips the hold: a wheel or button event, or any key on the UART console of the testbed (skip_on_console_key, set by the RP2350 main). Then it fades to the placeholder home screen (status bar with the battery percentage, list of unavailable features, last input event).
Check Passes when Currently on the bench display panel initialised passes storage card identified and the FAT/exFAT volume mounted; writes stay locked (the settings save opens them for /.neupod only, see Bluetooth) passes with a card battery MAX17048 ACKs at 0x36, VERSION 0x001X, cell voltage 2.5 to 4.6 V passes with a cell haptics DRV2605L ACKs at 0x5A, device ID 7; left in standby passes when fitted click wheel receiver starts, init packet sent, a valid frame arrives degraded (not wired, init packet unimplemented) audio the sink's stream runs: the audio core published its rate and served blocks (cannot detect the DAC: I2S is one-way) passes with the I2S sink; degraded with the null sink Bluetooth the radio driver is up and BTstack's HCI reaches the working state (local address read) passes on the Pico 2 W (stage 1; not yet seen on the board) Wi-Fi radio driver and lwIP are up (not: joined a network) passes on the Pico 2 W (W1; not yet seen on the board)

Deadlines: storage 4 s, battery and haptics 1.5 s, wheel 1.5 s, audio 0.5 s, radio 4.8 s (the radio check keeps waiting up to 12 s, so a slow Bluetooth start still upgrades its result). A check that misses its deadline is marked degraded and its later result is ignored (except that radio upgrade). I2C runs at 400 kHz.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text: capabilities_t (app/include/capabilities.h) holds a state (pending, ok, degraded) and a text per subsystem. The UI and later features read it (caps_available(CAP_STORAGE)); the input task, for instance, forwards wheel events only if the wheel check passed, so a floating unwired receiver cannot inject presses.

docs.title: Input sources and the testbed key map
docs.text:
All input reaches the UI as input_event_t through one queue, filled only by the input task (the sole caller of hal_input_poll() and of the console reader). Wheel-sourced events are forwarded only once the wheel passed its boot check (or when the wheel is a simulation, as on the host); other sources never depend on the wheel.

Source Keys UART console on the testbed (console_keys) w / k scroll up (counter-clockwise), s / j scroll down (+/-4 wheel positions = one list step); Enter or e = Select; a = Left; d = Right; p or Space = Play/Pause; m or Backspace = Menu; l = toggle Hold (the Pico rig has no Power key, ADR-0020) Host simulator window Up / Down arrows and the mouse wheel scroll; Enter = Select; Left / Right; Space or p = Play/Pause; Esc, Backspace or m = Menu; F1 = the Power key (hold it: 2 s toggles Hold, 10 s asks for a power-off, which the simulator only logs)

Any input event also skips the splash hold. The UI screens and their keys are described in UI. hal_input_reinit() failing (the init packet is still TODO(hw)) is not fatal: the wheel check passes if valid frames arrive within about 1.1 s, otherwise it is degraded ("not connected").

docs.title: Failure handling
docs.text:
• FreeRTOS stack overflow, malloc failure and configASSERT (also LVGL assertions) call neupod_panic(): the message including the task name goes out on the UART through a lock-free path, then the board halts, repeating the message and flashing the LED (2 = stack overflow, 3 = out of memory, 4 = assertion, 5 = other). On the Pico 2 W the only LED is behind the CYW43 chip, whose driver needs the running scheduler, so the LED code shows only for task-context failures; define NEUPOD_PANIC_LED_GPIO=<pin> for a board with a direct LED. A panic resets the audio core (RP2350) so nothing keeps playing, and in task context freezes every other task (UI included) except the idle task, the timer task and the radio worker, which the LED needs; tradeoff: the radio worker keeps running. From an interrupt or inside the kernel nothing blocking is possible, so there it is the UART message and a halt only.
  • Failing to create a permanent task or runtime object (UI, input, storage, monitor, queues, the I2C mutex) is fatal (neupod_panic, LED code 3); failing to create a boot-check task only degrades that capability.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
• RP2350: scripts/build.sh rp2350, flash neupod.elf; the UART shows the boot lines, a neuPod alive heartbeat every second and the 10 s statistics.
  • Host: scripts/build.sh host, then build/host/hal/host/neupod (SDL window if available; arrows/mouse wheel scroll, Enter/Space/Esc buttons) or neupod --run-ms 8000 --snapshots DIR (headless, writes splash.ppm and home.ppm; --splash-hold-ms N shortens the failure hold, the smoke test uses 1500). ctest --test-dir build/host runs it as runtime_smoke, writing build/host/snapshots/.

docs.title: Flashing
docs.text: scripts/flash.sh programs, verifies, resets and then explicitly resumes both cores; see scripts/README.md. (OpenOCD's reset otherwise leaves core 1 halted, so the audio core would not run.)

docs.title: What is stubbed
docs.text: AAC decoder (FLAC, MP3, ALAC and WAV play), prefetch (logs requests), home screen (placeholder), click-wheel receiver (pins unconfirmed), Bluetooth pairing and A2DP (stage 2, Bluetooth). Not yet measured on hardware with this architecture: block jitter under UI load, the panic LED, stack margins.

docs.title: microSD storage and its tests
docs.text: Phase 1 reads and writes the library on a microSD card over 4-bit SDIO, driven from a PIO program (not SPI). The firmware talks to it through hal_storage.h (card, raw sectors, mount) and the portable file API nfs.h (files and directories); see ADR-0006 and ADR-0008.

docs.title: Card format decision
docs.text:
• Project format: exFAT, 128 KB clusters, aligned to the card's allocation unit. Reasons: files over 4 GB, SDXC cards are exFAT natively, and large clusters keep the FAT small and reads sequential.
  • FAT32 must mount as a fallback. The Phase 1 card arrived as FAT32 and every test except the format test runs on it unchanged.
  • The layout is an MBR with one exFAT partition (type 07) starting at the card's allocation unit and a data area aligned the same way, which is what the SD Association formatter makes.
  • Do not reformat the card on a PC or phone. Operating-system formatters pick their own cluster size and ignore the card's alignment. If you must, use the SD Association's SD Memory Card Formatter, which keeps the alignment. The firmware only formats when you ask (test 9).
  • 128 KB clusters waste space on small files (cover art) but make audio-heavy libraries fast; the numbers are in ADR-0008 and should be revisited with the measured results below.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
From wiring-phase1.md (3.3 V, DAT0-DAT3 must be consecutive GPIOs, CLK is DAT0 - 2):

Signal GPIO CLK GP2 CMD GP3 DAT0 GP4 DAT1 GP5 DAT2 GP6 DAT3 GP7

docs.title: Library and resource use
docs.text:
• Driver: carlk3's no-OS-FatFS-SD-SDIO-SPI-RPi-Pico, release v3.6.2 (Apache-2.0), a git submodule in lib/. After cloning run git submodule update --init --recursive. Its FatFs is used on the RP2350 (the host build uses the vendored FatFs); the FatFs configuration is platforms/rp2350/ffconf/ffconf.h, kept identical to the host's by a build-time check.
  • PIO / DMA: the SD driver owns pio1 (two state machines), two DMA channels claimed dynamically, and shares DMA_IRQ_0. The Wi-Fi chip and the click-wheel receiver land on pio2. If something else has claimed a state machine on pio1 the card refuses to start with a clear error instead of misbehaving.
  • Clock: the PIO program needs 4 PIO cycles per SD clock, so the SDIO clock is clk_sys / (4 x divider) = 125 MHz / (4 x 2) = 15.625 MHz by default (an integer divider; see the observations below). It can be changed at run time (hal_storage_set_bus_clock).
  • High Speed: the card says 25 MHz in default-speed mode (CSD TRAN_SPEED 0x32). Faster clocks need the card switched to High Speed (command CMD6). The driver library never sends it; the HAL does (hal_storage_enable_high_speed) using the library's low-level calls, and refuses clocks above 25 MHz until it has succeeded.
  • Write safety: writes are locked by default. Only the tests that need them unlock writes, for as long as they run, and always lock again and delete their files (even after a failure or q). In the runtime firmware one other piece of code opens the lock: the settings save, for the length of one save and only for paths under /.neupod (an nfs write scope; Bluetooth). Before unlocking, a test reads 16 MB of the card twice and compares; test files are created exclusively (an existing file is never overwritten; the test stops and tells you).
  • Write-fault latch: the driver library ignores the card's status after a write and can leave the card waiting for data after a failed write. The HAL therefore checks the card status after every write, and after any failure refuses all further writes until the card is re-initialised; test cleanup re-initialises and remounts first, and if that is impossible it leaves writes locked and lists the files to delete by hand.
  • Free space is computed with a full scan of the FAT (the stored FAT32 hint is not trusted), so it is slow on a big FAT32 volume; the time is printed.
  • Stack: the main stack is 4 KB for the storage test (the most core 0's scratch RAM bank can hold); the lowest free stack seen is printed after each test.

docs.title: Playlists, play counts and On-The-Go (design review LB-7)
docs.text:
Two files besides ratings.bin, both written by the storage task under the same nfs write scope (/.neupod only), the same hardware write lock discipline, and always through a temp file that is synced and then renamed over the old one (the card does not rename over a file, so the old one is unlinked first; a power cut leaves the old file, or a complete temp file that the next read picks up; a partial temp file fails its check and is ignored). Only the builds with NEUPOD_ART_HIRES (hosted, Y2, PSRAM boards) keep them; the frozen Pico 2 W compiles them out.

File What Format Card refuses writes /.neupod/plays.bin (plays_store.[ch]) counted plays and "last played" per track, with the path, title and artist the smart lists show binary: NPPL, version 1, serial, count, entries (key = path + size hash as for ratings, plays u16, last u32, stamp u32, three length-prefixed strings), CRC-32. 128 entries; the fewest played goes first, a rated one last RAM only, retried every 30 s (plays_persistent()) /.neupod/otg.m3u8 (playlist_service.c) On-The-Go an ordinary UTF-8 playlist (#EXTM3U, #EXTINF:secs,Artist - Title, absolute path), ending in # end; at most 100 entries; add, remove and clear rewrite the whole file the add says "Card is write-protected" (nothing is kept in RAM)

A play is counted once per track start when half of it was actually heard (time spent playing, so a seek does not count), 30 s if its length is unknown, or when it ends by itself after 3 s (play_tracker.h). Paths of 96 bytes or more are not tracked in plays.bin. Ratings stay in ratings.bin (a hash): Top rated lists the tracks the plays store knows, which a rating of four stars or more adds (a rating made before this feature appears once the track is played or re-rated). .m3u / .m3u8 files are only read, from /, /Playlists and /Music (not their sub-folders).

docs.title: Music library index
docs.text:
Index format 3 (12 Nov 2026): sort keys skip a leading "A " / "An " as well as "The "; an older index is "needs rebuilding" and the Music lists rebuild it by themselves. Playlists add two files under /.neupod (below).

The Music screens read an index of /Music that the firmware builds on the card itself (ADR-0017; screens: UI).

  • Where and how. /.neupod/lib/: 13 immutable files plus a manifest (about 8 MB for 100,000 tracks, roughly 90 bytes a track), each written once per build, the manifest last. A build goes to /.neupod/lib.tmp/, is synced, and replaces lib with two renames (lib to lib.old, lib.tmp to lib); a power cut leaves the old library or the new one (lib_recover() settles an interrupted swap the first time the index is opened after boot). A failed or cancelled build deletes lib.tmp and leaves the old library.
  • Writes. The index is the second thing in the firmware that unlocks card writes, after the settings save: only the storage task, only for the length of a build, and only under /.neupod (the nfs write scope; every folder-tree change is a real nfs_mkdir / nfs_unlink / nfs_rename, which nfs itself gates; /Music is never written). Nothing else in the library writes. A write-protected card is answered up front with "Library needs a writable card", before anything is attempted; a card that is full says so (Card is full).
  • When. The first time a list is opened with no index on the card, and Music > Update Library; never in the background, and only with nothing playing (the scanner borrows the audio core's decoder memory as its scratch, 99 KB, and refuses to start while anything plays or is paused). A Play press, a folder listing, Cancel or Menu stop it at the next file. Shutting the firmware down during a build is safe for the same reason a power cut is.
  • What it costs. Static RAM (RP2350 Release, measured): nothing for the reader and the row window (they share the Files screen's 20 KB listing buffer); +760 B for the service's bookkeeping and path cache, the queue and the resume path (free SRAM 14,504 B to 13,744 B). Flash: +40.6 KB: the library itself (about 28 KB of scanner, reader, sort and collation that L1 did not link yet) and about 13 KB for the lists, the service, the range queue and the screens. Reading: browsing keeps the audio ring topped up between rows; the reader holds 11 files open and a 4 x 2 KB page cache.
  • How long a scan takes. Host figure (POSIX files in the simulator, warm cache): 276 tracks in 131 ms, 1,016 tracks in 322 ms; L1's 100,000-file run on a FatFs disk image: 12 s. On the card it is not measured yet (the bench has not run it). Estimate from the ADR's costs (0.2-0.4 ms per directory entry, 10-20 ms to open and parse a file) plus about 60 small index and run files to create: about 260 FLACs in 5 to 8 seconds, 5,000 tracks in about 1.5 minutes, 100,000 in half an hour. The progress screen counts files; the sort and write at the end add a second or two without a counter.
  • The Y2 testbed. The Y2 firmware opens the card read-only (O_RDONLY) and only reopens it O_RDWR | O_SYNC while the library or the settings store holds the write lock, so no change to the Y2's storage is needed for the index to be written, and none was made. What it does need: the card's write-protect switch off (a write-protected card is opened read-only and the screen says Library needs a writable card); nothing else mounting the same card at the same time (the firmware's FatFs and a kernel filesystem driver writing one volume would corrupt it; the Y2's rootfs does not mount the card: its mdev.conf only sets the node's permissions and its fstab has no card entry; the rescue diag.sh is the one thing that mounts it, on demand, so check before adding an automounter); and patience, since O_SYNC makes every write wait for the card (a build is many small writes, so the Y2 will be slower than the estimate above). The boot line read-only is the default lock, not a mount option.

docs.title: Rules carried into the final board (3 Nov 2026)
docs.text:
• SD clock from integer dividers only.
  • Multi-block reads capped at 128 blocks (NEUPOD_SDIO_MAX_READ_BLOCKS, platforms/rp2350/hal/hal_storage.c): in v3.6.2 a 256-block read writes the DMA list terminator one entry past dma_blocks[]. To be reported upstream to carlk3 (no-OS-FatFS-SD-SDIO-SPI-RPi-Pico).
  • A GPIO-controlled load switch on card VDD is a final-board requirement, so a card wedged mid-transfer can be power-cycled.

docs.title: Memory allocation policy
docs.text:
The newlib heap is only about 33 KB (static RAM fills the rest) and the Pico SDK's malloc wrapper panics on failure instead of returning NULL (to be replaced by a wrapper that returns NULL and logs, per the design response of 3 Nov 2026; not built). FatFs with FF_USE_LFN 3 allocates scratch buffers as large as a cluster (dir_clear, up to 32 KB; 128 KB clusters on large exFAT cards) and relies on NULL to halve the request, so the first mkdir on the bench ended in "Out of memory".

app/storage/ff_alloc.c therefore replaces the library's ffsystem.c (the RP2350 build removes it from the library's source list in platforms/rp2350/CMakeLists.txt; lib/ is untouched, the host build uses the same file). ff_memalloc returns NULL for anything above NEUPOD_FF_ALLOC_MAX_BYTES (4 KB, app/storage/ff_alloc.h) and otherwise calls the real, non-panicking malloc, so FatFs falls back to a 4 KB buffer or its window buffer. Mutex functions are not provided: FF_FS_REENTRANT is 0 and the build fails if it is turned on. Host test: tests/test_fatfs.c.

Besides FatFs the only newlib-heap callers in the firmware image are the Bluetooth firmware download (about 1 KB, once at boot) and newlib's one-off stdio setup; core 1 never allocates (checked by tools/check_core1_closure.py).

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
git submodule update --init --recursive
export PICO_SDK_PATH=$HOME/pico/pico-sdk
scripts/build.sh rp2350
scripts/flash.sh rp2350 storage_test
scripts/console.sh      # type the keys here (the PC's serial console), not on the Pico
Key Test Writes? 1 Detect: card identification, CID/CSD/SD status, sector 0 No 2 Mount: file system type, cluster size, label, serial, total/free space No 3 List: recursive listing of the root, depth 2, capped at 200 entries No 4 Integrity: 16 MB pseudo-random file round trip across a remount, then a 2 MB raw-sector round trip inside a file the test allocated Under /neupod-test/ 5 Sequential speed at 512 B, 4 KB, 32 KB, 128 KB blocks, read and write Under /neupod-test/ 6 2000 random 4 KB reads (latency average/min/max/p99), with and without fast seek Allocates under /neupod-test/ 7 Streaming: 32 KB every 20 ms for 10 s, counts missed deadlines Allocates under /neupod-test/ 8 Clock sweep: steps the SDIO clock up until an error, suggests a setting. Run it on its own; it needs /neupod-test not to exist beforehand Raw sectors inside one file under /neupod-test/ 9 Format the card: MBR plus one exFAT partition (needs typing YES) Erases everything a Runs 1-7 and prints a summary; never runs 8 or 9 as above q Stop the running test c Clean up leftover test files: lists /neupod-test/, then (after y) deletes only pattern.bin, raw.bin, speed.bin, sweep.bin and the directory if empty; never part of a Deletes under /neupod-test/

Before any write test the card must have at least the test's size plus 64 MB free. Everything is written under /neupod-test/, which is created if missing and removed again if it was created by the test. A full run of 1-8 takes a few minutes (estimates: test 4 about 15 s, test 5 about 40 s, test 6 about 10 s, test 7 about 15 s, test 8 about 20 s); test 9 on a 64 GB card can take a minute or more.

Test 8 allocates one contiguous file with the file system at the safe clock, then at each higher clock does only a read-only soak (4 MB read twice plus 100 status queries) followed by raw writes inside that file; the file system is not touched until the clock is back to normal. A failure at a test clock cannot damage the file system, only that file.

Test 9 shows the card name and capacity, the current volume (type, label, space used), warns that all data will be erased, including other partitions such as a Linux root file system, and only continues if you type exactly YES and press Enter. It writes a partition table with one exFAT partition starting at the card's allocation-unit boundary, creates exFAT with 128 KB clusters aligned the same way, and labels it NEUPOD; then it remounts and shows test 2's output.

On the PC, scripts/build.sh host builds the same menu as build/host/hal/host/storage_test over a disk image (NEUPOD_DISK_IMAGE) and a files directory (NEUPOD_FS_ROOT, default build/host/fsroot). Mount, raw-sector, clock and format tests are skipped there.

docs.title: Confirmed card facts (stage 1, on the bench)
docs.text: Item Value Card SanDisk SU64G, SDXC, 124,735,488 sectors (63.86 GB), writable CID MID 0x03, OID "SD", PRV 8.0, PSN 0x1AC15256, date 2012-07 Bus 4-bit at 12.5 MHz; CSD v2, TRAN_SPEED 0x32 (25 MHz) SD status Speed class C10, UHS U1, allocation unit 4096 KiB Layout MBR, partition 1 type 0x0C (FAT32) Seen by FatFs (before test 9) Raspberry Pi OS card: 256 MB FAT32 partition "bootfs" (2 KB clusters); the Linux root partition is invisible to FatFs After test 9 (2026-11-02) MBR, one partition type 0x07 at sector 8192; exFAT, 128 KB clusters, label NEUPOD, 63.85 GB free; format took 656 ms Timing init 122 ms, one sector read 6 ms

docs.title: Measured results (bench, 2026-11-02, SanDisk SU64G, Phase 1 breadboard)
docs.text:
MB = 1,000,000 bytes. Test 5 uses a pre-allocated 32 MB file; random reads are 2000 × 4 KB.

Measurement FAT32 "bootfs", 2 KB clusters, 12.5 MHz FAT32, 25 MHz exFAT, 128 KB clusters, 15.625 MHz (current) Integrity (test 4): 16 MB file + 2 MB raw PASS, 0 mismatches PASS, 0 mismatches PASS, 0 mismatches Sequential write, best 4.39 MB/s (32 KB) 8.45 MB/s (32 KB) 6.50 MB/s (128 KB) Sequential read, best 2.84 MB/s 3.82 MB/s 7.28 MB/s (128 KB) Random 4 KB read, plain seek, avg 21.0 ms 18.7 ms 1.27 ms (p99 1.59 ms) Random 4 KB read, fast seek, avg / p99 1.47 / 2.00 ms — 1.26 / 1.55 ms Streaming 32 KB / 20 ms, 10 s 0 misses, headroom 20% 0 misses, headroom 46% 0 misses, worst 4.9 ms, headroom 76% Clock sweep (test 8) all steps to 31.25 MHz OK (HS) leaving HS failed; later run failed at 25 MHz on response CRC 10.4 and 15.6 MHz OK; HS switch failed (response CRC)

Observations and open items:

  • exFAT with 128 KB clusters fixed the slow reads. On FAT32 with 2 KB clusters FatFs splits every transfer at cluster boundaries (at most 4 sectors per disk call), and the driver pays a read command plus a stop command per call. With 128 KB clusters, reads went from 3.8 to 7.3 MB/s, and random reads no longer need fast seek (1.27 ms either way).
  • Streaming is comfortable: 32 KB every 20 ms (1.64 MB/s, about 2.7× FLAC 24/96) with 76 % headroom.
  • Library bug, worked around: carlk3 v3.6.2 rp2040_sdio_rx_start() writes its DMA list terminator one entry past dma_blocks[SDIO_MAX_BLOCKS * 2] for a 256-block read, wedging the driver. FAT32 with 2 KB clusters never triggers it; exFAT with 128 KB clusters does on every 128 KB read. The HAL splits reads into chunks of at most 128 blocks (guarded_read in hal_storage.c), and a failed read latches the write fault so the card is re-initialised before any further write. Worth reporting upstream.
  • Command-response CRC errors (open): the same responses are misread identically every time: CMD13 calculated 0x7c vs received 0x7e, CMD17 0xcc vs 0xce, CMD55 0x64 vs 0x66. They always differ in the last CRC7 bit. They appear around clock changes and the CMD6 (High Speed) sequence, at fractional dividers (12.5, 20.8, 25 MHz) and once at 15.625 MHz during CMD6. They never appeared during data tests 4–7 at 15.625 MHz. They look deterministic (a response-sampling or decoding issue in the PIO/driver path) rather than noise. Not yet root-caused. Because of them, the default is 15.625 MHz in default-speed mode and High Speed is not used.
  • The 10 MB/s USB mass-storage target is not reachable at clk_sys 125 MHz with this PIO program (4 PIO cycles per SD clock → 31.25 MHz maximum, High Speed only). Best measured: 6.5 MB/s write, 7.3 MB/s read. Open item, no decision (options: higher clk_sys, a different SDIO PIO program, or accept a slower sync).
  • Leaving High Speed mode needs care: the card is quieted at the current clock (open write closed, not busy), the clock lowered, and only then is the card reset and re-identified, with up to three tries; the sweep test fails if the card cannot be brought back.

docs.title: Failure checklist
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause / action Card ignores the first identification after a debugger reset A reset mid-transfer can leave the card in a data state; a power cycle always fixes it. hal_storage_init() makes up to three attempts; before the 2nd and 3rd it sends four CMD12 (stop transmission: no data, harmless to an idle card, ends an open read or write-multiple) at the 400 kHz identification clock, reads each response, waits 50 ms and logs storage: card did not identify, wake-up attempt N. Nothing is written. A missing card still fails in well under a second (about 0.65 s in all, 0.5 s more than with a single attempt); it is called once at boot, never in a loop Test 1: NO_CARD or init timeout Card not fully inserted, 3.3 V missing, CLK/CMD/DAT wiring (GP2-GP7), no pull-up on CMD, card not powered CRC errors, or tests pass at 12.5 MHz but fail higher Clock too fast for the wiring: lower the clock, shorten wires, check pull-ups on CMD and DAT0-3 Test 2: NO_FILESYSTEM No FAT/exFAT volume (blank card, unusual partition layout), or the file system configuration is wrong (sector size not 512, exFAT disabled) Test 2 slow Free-space scan on a big FAT32 volume is slow by nature; it is printed separately Slow random reads (test 6) Small clusters or a fragmented file; compare plain and fast seek Streaming misses deadlines Read time varies: look at the worst read time; lower the clock only if errors appear, otherwise raise it Test 4 mismatches Bus errors that slipped past the CRC, or a bad card; repeat at a lower clock Test 8 stops at 25 MHz / "High Speed switch failed" The card refused High Speed, or a command response failed its CRC (see the open item above); keep the default SDIO "Timed out waiting for data block" on large reads The library's 256-block DMA bug: make sure reads go through the HAL's chunked guarded_read Card unreadable on a PC after test 9 Check the partition table with a PC tool: one partition, type 07, starting at the allocation-unit boundary; see ADR-0008 "writes locked until re-init" or "write fault" A write failed or the card status after a write was bad; the card was reset, check wiring and clock A test says a file already exists An earlier run was interrupted; delete /neupod-test on a PC and run again

docs.title: Wheel input widgets
docs.text: One library for every place the UI needs the user to enter something with a click wheel: text (passwords, names, search), numbers, levels, choices and dates. Code: app/ui/input/. The model of each widget (app/include/wheel_input.h, wheel_input.c) is pure C with no LVGL and is unit tested on the PC (tests/test_wheel_input.c); the view (app/ui/input/ui_input.c) draws it with LVGL and feeds it the input.

docs.title: Key semantics (the same in every widget)
docs.text:
Input Meaning scroll change what is under the cursor: the glyph in the ring, the value, the highlighted choice, the field. Steps arrive already accelerated by the UI frame Select choose or type: types the highlighted key, ticks a multi-choice item, picks the choice, goes to the next date field Menu back: backspace when there is text, otherwise cancel (a number, slider or choice cancels at once; a slider restores its old value); held 0.6 s it clears the whole text Play/Pause confirm and close Left / Right the mode chip of a text entry, or the date/time field

A modal swallows every button (Menu never pops the screen underneath by accident).

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text: Widget Request kind Result in wi_value_t Notes Text entry WI_K_TEXT text the letter ring (design review 3.7, IN-1): a field box with a caret at the top, a ring of nine glyphs (the current one Big in the accent, its neighbours smaller and greyer) turned by the wheel, and mode chips abc / ABC / 123 / #!? / space / del under it, switched with Left / Right (a charset of digits or hex offers only 123 and del; space only for free text); Select types the glyph in the ring (on the space chip a space, on del deletes one), Menu deletes (hold clears), Play is done. A masked password shows the character just typed for 800 ms, then a bullet. The text always grows at its end (no cursor). max_chars (code points), max_bytes, charset ANY / DIGITS / HEX; UTF-8 safe buffer; initial text Search WI_K_TEXT with search = true text like text, and change fires after every edit so the caller can filter a list live. A suggestions row is not built; the callback is where it would hook in Number WI_K_NUMBER number the value Big and centred with a bar under it and min / max in Small at its ends (IN-2); min, max, step, decimals (fixed point, value in units of 10^-decimals), unit ("dB", "min", "%"); scroll steps are multiplied by the wheel acceleration; clamps Slider WI_K_SLIDER number a number with a bar and a live change callback; cancel sends the original value through change so the preview is reverted. Settings > Display (backlight) uses it Choice WI_K_PICKER pick a plain list; single choice from items[count]; multi = true makes Select tick items and the result is mask Date and time WI_K_DATETIME dt the active field in the accent colour (underlined) with the name of every field under it (Day, Month, Year, Hour, Min); has_date / has_time; fields day, month, year (2000 to 2099), hour, minute; the day follows the month and leap years; Select walks the fields and confirms on the last one Letter jump ui_letter_overlay_* + wi_letterjump_* n/a not a modal: an overlay on a sorted list. While the wheel is turned fast (6 steps within 400 ms) a box shows the initial of the item under the cursor; it hides 700 ms later. wi_letter_first_index() finds the first item for a letter (binary search). Files shows it today; the library will use it

docs.title: API
docs.text:
#include "ui_input.h"

static void name_done(void *ctx, bool ok, const wi_value_t *v) { if (ok) use(v->text); }

ui_input_open(&(wi_request_t){
    .kind = WI_K_TEXT, .title = "Network name", .initial = "", .max_chars = 32, .done = name_done });

ui_input_open() pushes the modal screen on the UI stack (one at a time: it returns false while another is open) and calls done(ctx, ok, &value) exactly once, before the modal closes. Two rules follow from that:

  • Do not open the next modal from inside done. The modal is popped after the callback returns, which would pop the new one. Record the result and open the next step from the owning screen's tick (the Wi-Fi screen does this for SSID, then security, then password).
  • Strings in the request only have to live until the call returns; the result is copied into wi_value_t.

Live filtering for a future library search: search = true plus change = filter_list where the callback sets the list's filter text and refreshes the list model.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Models are small structs (the text model is 90 bytes). LVGL objects exist only while a modal is open. A covered screen can free its rebuildable objects (suspend / resume on ui_screen_t; the list widget frees all its rows) and a modal calls ui_frame_suspend_top() before building itself, so a modal opened over a list does not add its size on top of the list's. LVGL pool use on the host (64-bit objects, pool 72 KB, about 63 KB usable), read from the tour (ctest -R input_tour), with the Extras > Input widgets list underneath:

Widget LVGL pool used while open Without a covering list text, password, search 46.8 KB the same number, slider 44.9 to 45.4 KB picker, multi choice 59.8 KB (a list in a list) date/time 46.4 KB the list screen alone 57.4 KB

The firmware uses 32-bit pointers, so the objects are smaller there; the figure to read on the board is the lvgl_mem= line of the monitor.

docs.title: Demo and tests
docs.text:
• Extras > Input widgets opens each widget and shows the last result.
  • neupod --tour-input --snapshots DIR (ctest input_tour) walks through every widget and writes one snapshot each.
  • ctest -R wheel_input runs the model tests: typing, cursor, page switching, maximum length, masking, charsets, UTF-8, cancel and confirm, number clamping and acceleration, picker wrap and clamp, multi choice, date validity including leap years, letter-jump index calculation.
  • Not built: typing directly on the host keyboard as a shortcut (the host key map reserves most letters for the wheel keys); the testbed UART keys drive the widgets like the wheel.

docs.title: UI mock-ups
docs.text:
Text, number, level, choice and date entry with the click wheel is one library: Wheel input widgets. Wi-Fi screens: Wi-Fi.

Design review of 12 November 2026 (colour tokens, type scale, new screens, owner decisions): design review; its backlog is in Backlog.

Target: the Phase 1 panel, 320×240 landscape. Each screen is an original drawing at the panel's native size (SVG, viewBox="0 0 320 240"); the look follows the classic click-wheel player layout — split menu with artwork, blue selection bar — lightly modernised. These are design intent, not screenshots of any existing firmware.

Click-wheel vocabulary used below: Menu (top button, goes back), Select (centre), Play/Pause (bottom), Left / Right (previous / next), scroll (finger on the ring).

docs.title: Main menu
docs.text:
• Scroll moves the selection bar through Music, Podcasts, Photos, Extras, Settings, Shuffle Songs, Now Playing. Scroll acceleration follows the Rockbox constants (4 counts per step, velocity-based acceleration).
  • Select opens the highlighted item. Menu does nothing at the top level.
  • Play/Pause toggles playback without leaving the menu; the right pane shows the current track's artwork and title, or a clock when nothing is playing.
  • Left / Right skip tracks in the background.

docs.title: Library — artists
docs.text:
• Full-width list; scroll bar on the right shows position in long lists. Fast scrolling shows a letter overlay so a 100k-track library is navigable.
  • Select descends (artist → albums → tracks); Menu ascends one level.
  • Right on an artist jumps to All Albums for that artist; Left returns to the previous level without animation. (Design intent: Right / Left skip tracks in the built lists, as everywhere else.)
  • The same template serves Albums, Songs, Genres, Composers, Playlists and Podcasts. Built: see Music lists.

docs.title: Music lists
docs.text:
The Music screens read the library index on the card (ADR-0017, how it is stored and built). Every list is the same screen: a full-width list with the usual scroll acceleration; the first line of a row is the name, the right-hand text is the second fact (an album's artist, a song's artist, the length of a track in an album, the number of songs in an artist's album); a chevron marks a row that opens another list.

List Rows Select Artists album artists, collated (a leading "The " ignored, accents folded, symbols, then digits, then letters) the artist: All Songs, then its albums Albums every album by name, the album artist on the right the album's songs in track order (disc, track, title) Songs every song in title order plays it Genres genre names the genre: All Songs, then its artists Compilations albums flagged as compilations (or by "Various Artists") the album's songs artist / genre All Songs first All Songs lists every song of the artist (album by album) or of the genre (album order)

Select on a song plays it and queues the whole list it was chosen from: an album in track order, an artist's songs, a genre, or all songs, starting at that song, with the earlier songs kept for Previous. Gapless playback, repeat, shuffle (Settings) and resume work as for a folder; Now Playing shows n of N. A file the player cannot play (AAC, more than two channels, damaged) is listed greyed; Select shows why (Can't play: unsupported codec (AAC)) and auto-advance skips it. Home > Shuffle Songs plays the whole library in a random order (every song once; the Shuffle setting is not changed). Playlists still say None yet.

Two-line rows and the album header (LB-1, LB-3). Lists of songs (Songs, an artist's All Songs, a genre's All Songs) show two lines per row, 40 / 60 px, five rows: the title in Body and Artist . Album in Small ink2 below (the artist no longer sits at the right, where it collided with long titles); the focused row's two lines are tickers. The status bar shows the count with a thousands comma (1,204). An album opens with a header (art 64 / 96 px, the album in the large font, Artist . 2019, 3 songs . 9:41 . FLAC, a hairline) over the track rows 3 Title with the length at the right; a song the player cannot play is greyed with its codec in brackets (Carrier Wave (AAC)), so the reason is visible before pressing. The status bar's left slot holds the album's name. The header's facts come with the album's info request (lvw_info_t: artist, first year, summed length, common codec; read from the first 100 songs); its art is decoded by the art service (see Now Playing art).

Fast scroll (LB-2). While the wheel spins a long list past the acceleration threshold, a dark tile with the letter of the focused row appears at the top right and an index rail runs down the right edge (A to Z, every second letter in ink3, the current letter in ink; the letters next to it make room). It stays while the wheel moves and fades out in 150 ms once the wheel has rested for 250 ms. It never covers the selection bar's row text beyond the right 14 px of the first lines. The letter is the first letter of the row's collation key (lib_collate_key(): a leading "The " is ignored, accents are folded, a number or symbol is #), so the rail agrees with the sort. The sort ignores "The " and accents already; "A " / "An " are not ignored yet (see Backlog). The same component (ui_rail.c, ui_letter_overlay_*) is used by Files, which sorts by plain name.

A long list never holds more than a few screens of rows in memory: the storage task fills a window of 16 rows around the selection, and a row that has not arrived yet shows ... for the moment it takes. Both resolution profiles use the same screens (the 480x360 layout audit runs on every snapshot of the library_tour).

No index yet. The first Artists / Albums / Songs / Genres / Compilations / Shuffle Songs opens the card's /Music and builds the index (a one-off; Music > Update Library rebuilds it later, for example after adding albums). Progress is a screen of three lines: Building library... with busy dots, n songs found and Select to cancel (Cancel or Menu leaves the old library untouched). It runs only with nothing playing: while music plays it says Stop playback to update the library. Other messages: Library needs a writable card (the card is write-protected, or the card refused the write), Card is full, Card read error, No card; each offers Select to try again. Update Library ends with Library updated and the counts.

docs.title: Now playing
docs.text:
Built in phase 2 of the design review (NP-1 to NP-5; mock-ups np-* there). Page 1:

  • Art (112 / 168 px) at the left; to its right Title (large), Artist (Body, ink2) and Album . Year (Small, ink3). A file with no title tag shows its file name as the title and its folder as the artist. Title, artist and album are tickers: wider than the column, they scroll (the owner's rule above). While something other than plain playing is going on the third line says it instead: Opening..., the error text (red), Finished, the MD5 check and its verdict.
  • Under the text the pill row: a format pill (accent_soft, FLAC 16/44.1; on a Bluetooth output the codec that leaves the box: SBC 44.1, SBC-XQ, AAC) and an outline pill with the output (Wired, or the headset's name, cut with dots when long). A test tone shows TEST SIGNAL.
  • The progress bar is 4 px, elapsed on the left (a pause glyph before it while paused), remaining on the right (-~ for an estimated MP3 length), and a quiet ink3 word in the middle while either is on: shuffle, repeat, repeat 1, shuffle . repeat.
  • The volume strip at the bottom: Volume -18 dB (or Headset 62% on a headset with absolute volume, same 0..127 scale) and a 4 px ink2 bar over the right 55 %. A headset left at 0 % while playing reads Headset 0% . silent in amber (the old "headset volume 0 %" hint).
  • Status bar: n of m at the left, Now Playing in the middle.
  • Scroll adjusts volume. Select: a short press opens page 2; hold Select (about 0.5 s, with a haptic tick) is seek mode. Play/Pause toggles; Left / Right previous / next track; hold Left / Right scans the track at 10x and applies on release (the old behaviour). Menu returns to the list the track was chosen from (in seek mode it cancels the seek first).

Seek mode (NP-2). The pills, the album line and the volume strip give way to the seek time in the Big font (amber), the progress bar becomes 6 px amber (soft amber track) with a knob, and the hint Scroll: seek . Select: go . Menu: cancel takes the bottom line. The wheel moves the target (about 1/60 of the track per step, 1 to 30 s); Select applies it (one restart of the track at that frame) and leaves seek mode; Menu drops it. Nothing is applied by the wheel resting, and a seek mode left alone for 10 s is cancelled (so a forgotten seek never keeps the wheel; the old 3 s fallback is gone). A track that cannot seek (a FLAC without a seek table, the MD5 check) answers the hold with the toast Seek not available and stays on volume. The volume HUD shows while seek mode hides the strip. Logic: ui_npc_* in ui_logic.c (ui_npc_select_down / _up, ui_npc_menu, tick), host-tested in ui_logic. The old "Select toggles volume / seek" path is gone.

Page 2 (NP-3). Small art (64 / 96) and title, Artist . Album, then the star rating (five stars, lit ones accent): wheel up from the first row focuses the stars (a soft box behind them), the wheel then sets 0 to 5 stars, Select or Menu returns to the rows. Rows: Shuffle (Off / Songs), Repeat (Off / One / All), Gapless (On / Off), each toggled by Select (the same settings as Settings), Add to playlist (phase 4) (greyed; Select says Playlists in phase 4), Go to album and Go to artist (open that album / artist in the library with the track's own ids: the storage task keeps the album and album-artist id of the last two library tracks it resolved, library_track_ids(); greyed with Not in the library when the track plays from a folder or is a compilation, which has no album artist). Menu goes back to page 1. Page 2 needs a playing file; if playback stops under it, it closes. Ratings are saved on the card (/.neupod/ratings.bin, ratings_store.[ch]), keyed by file path and size so a rebuilt library keeps them; saved by the storage task under the settings store's write scope (confined to /.neupod), loaded when the card is ready. On a write-protected or failing card they stay in RAM and are written as soon as the card allows (retry every 30 s); up to 128 tracks (the least recently rated is dropped). The file is rewritten in place: a power cut during a save loses the ratings (the CRC makes it load as empty), nothing else.

Volume HUD (NP-4). A volume change while another screen is on top (the Y2's side keys, the headset's own volume, anything that moves the player's volume) shows the HUD strip for 1.2 s: Volume -18 dB or Headset 62% with the bar (update_volume_hud(), ui_frame.c; it polls player_volume_att() and bt_volume_get()). Screens that draw the volume themselves (Now Playing page 1 outside seek mode, Test tone) set ui_screen_t.shows_volume and get no HUD. Not shown while the screen is off or Hold is on, nor when the volume in use changes (a headset taking over). List scrolling is unchanged: the wheel still only scrolls.

Bluetooth link lost. Unchanged ADR-0019 behaviour, new words: playback pauses on the drop and stays on Bluetooth; when the five minutes of automatic reconnecting end with the headset still away the toast says Couldn't reconnect - paused (bt_service_gave_up_seq()).

  • On Bluetooth output the format pill reads the negotiated codec: SBC 44.1, or SBC-XQ when the headset accepted a bitpool above 53 (the source format is not shown then). A track that is not 44.1 kHz cannot be played on Bluetooth yet and is refused with "not supported on Bluetooth" (see Bluetooth).

docs.title: Album browser
docs.text:
The flat Cover Flow built in phase 4c (LB-6) replaces this mock-up's 3D carousel, see Cover Flow.

  • Dark full-screen carousel of album artwork; the centre album is enlarged with a reflection.
  • Scroll flips through albums with acceleration; Select opens the centre album's track list; Menu returns to the library.
